steps/3.description: FLVCR1 is expressed widely but at markedly different levels across tissues, being most abundant in the retina, followed by the posterior columns of the spinal cord, the cerebellum, and other CNS regions. The gradient itself has been measured as Flvcr1 mRNA in wild-type mouse tissue; no equivalent human measurement is available in the cited literature. This expression gradient is proposed to explain the disease's characteristic dual sensory phenotype: the retina, with the highest FLVCR1 expression, is vulnerable to even partial loss of heme-export function and is affected in essentially all patients, while the posterior columns require more severe loss of function to cross the pathogenic threshold and are therefore only affected in a subset of patients.

evidence.snippet: These results suggest that aberrant FLVCR1 causes a selective degeneration of a subpopulation of neurons in the retina and the posterior columns of the spinal cord via dysregulation of heme or iron homeostasis.
evidence.explanation: Directly attributes retinal (and posterior column) neuronal degeneration to FLVCR1-dependent heme/iron dysregulation.

steps/4.description: Heme toxicity in the highly FLVCR1-expressing retina drives selective degeneration of photoreceptors, producing the progressive pigmentary retinopathy characteristic of the disease.

evidence.snippet: Splice-site FLVCR1 variants may result in the translation of some fully functional FLVCR1 protein product which is sufficient for tissues in which FLVCR1 is expressed at a lower level (posterior columns and cerebellum), but which is insufficient to protect against the toxic effects of excess intracellular heme in tissues which express FLVCR1 highly (retina).
evidence.explanation: States the genotype-phenotype hypothesis that this node is about, in the same terms the node uses. It is an explicit conjecture ("may result in") built on a single reported patient, and the same paper says it "suggest[s] a hypothesis" whose association would still need to "be proven" -- which is why the node is named and described as a proposed, currently unproven mechanism rather than established fact.

evidence.snippet: We suggest an association between intronic splice-site variants in FLVCR1 and the absence of posterior column degeneration and suggest a hypothesis to explain this observation. Should this association be proven, it would provide valuable prognostic information for patients.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own framing of the residual-function model as an unproven hypothesis, recorded here so the node's epistemic status is explicit rather than implied.

steps/5.description: A proposed, currently unproven explanation for FLVCR1-related retinopathy without ataxia: splice-site FLVCR1 variants (e.g., c.1092+5G>A) may permit low-level production of correctly spliced, functional transcript despite triggering predominant exon skipping and a frameshift/premature stop codon on the majority of transcripts. Such residual functional protein would, on this hypothesis, be sufficient to protect the lower-FLVCR1-expressing posterior columns and cerebellum from heme toxicity while remaining insufficient to protect the higher-expressing retina. The suggestion rests on one 32-year-old patient plus two previously reported carriers of the same variant (aged 9 and 34); no functional assay of residual FLVCR1 protein from a splice allele has been reported, the authors note that the effects of deep splice-site changes are difficult to predict, and the residual-protein step is itself inferred from the embryonic lethality of the mouse null.

evidence.snippet: Inversion recovery MRIs of the spinal cord in affected individuals demonstrate a hyperintense signal in the posterior columns.
evidence.explanation: Direct imaging evidence of posterior column pathology in affected individuals from the original clinical description of the disorder.

steps/6.description: In patients whose FLVCR1 variants sufficiently impair heme export in lower-expressing tissues, heme toxicity also drives degeneration of the proprioceptive sensory neurons and axons of the spinal cord posterior columns, producing progressive sensory ataxia. Spinal cord MRI shows a hyperintense signal in the posterior columns of affected individuals. The mode of neuronal death here has not been characterized -- no cited source reports apoptosis, caspase activation, or another specific death pathway in posterior column neurons -- so no death-process term is annotated on this node.

edges/2.description: Loss of FLVCR1-mediated heme export prevents cytoplasmic heme from being exported out of the cell.

edges/3.description: Heme toxicity is only pathogenic in cells that both rely on FLVCR1 export and cannot compensate through alternative heme-handling pathways; the severity of this toxicity across tissues tracks FLVCR1 expression level.

edges/4.description: The retina's high FLVCR1 expression makes photoreceptors vulnerable to heme toxicity from even partial loss-of-function variants, explaining why retinopathy occurs in essentially all patients.

edges/5.description: The posterior columns' lower FLVCR1 expression requires more severe loss-of-function variants to cross the pathogenic heme-toxicity threshold, explaining why ataxia is absent in some patients.

edges/6.description: In the Isolated Retinopathy subtype, residual FLVCR1 function in the posterior columns is proposed to mitigate (rather than drive) this node -- the hypothesized basis for absence of ataxia despite biallelic FLVCR1 variants.

evidence.snippet: we identified a single-nucleotide coding variant in the feline leukemia virus subgroup C cellular receptor 1 (FLVCR1), a gene encoding a heme-transporter protein
evidence.explanation: Original gene-identification study establishing FLVCR1 as the heme-transporter gene mutated in PCARP.

genes/0.notes: FLVCR1 (feline leukemia virus subgroup C receptor 1) encodes a 12-transmembrane-domain heme exporter of the major facilitator superfamily. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause FLVCR1-related retinopathy with or without ataxia. Because Flvcr1-null mice die in mid-gestation, the authors of the 2018 case report infer that all reported human disease-causing variants are likely to permit translation of some functional FLVCR1 protein.

evidence.snippet: Symptoms of ataxia begin in the third decade in PCARP: this represents a therapeutic window to treat the CNS with gene therapy before the onset of posterior column degeneration.
evidence.explanation: Source for the proposed therapeutic window described in the notes. The claim is the authors' proposal for a gene-therapy approach that does not exist yet, not a demonstrated treatment effect, so it bears on this supportive-care entry only through the notes that record why a disease-modifying option is still being argued for.

treatments/0.description: Supportive low-vision aids and rehabilitation for the retinopathy.

treatments/1.description: Physical and occupational therapy for gait training and mobility aids to manage progressive sensory ataxia in patients with the PCARP subtype.

treatments/2.description: Genetic counseling for autosomal recessive inheritance, carrier detection, and family planning.

evidence.snippet: During development Foxe3 is expressed in all undifferentiated lens tissues, and is turned off upon fiber cell differentiation
evidence.explanation: Establishes Foxe3 as a lens-specific developmental transcription factor required for proper lens formation.

evidence.snippet: Foxe3 had been shown to play a crucial role in vertebrate lens formation and this gene is one of the earliest integrators of several signaling pathways that cooperate to form a lens
evidence.explanation: Reviews the central role of FOXE3 in integrating lens developmental signaling pathways.

evidence.snippet: it indicates a possible critical role for FOXE3 very early in the lens developmental program, perhaps earlier than any role recognized elsewhere for this gene
evidence.explanation: Suggests FOXE3 plays a very early role in lens development, consistent with aphakia as the null phenotype.

steps/1.description: FOXE3 is a forkhead transcription factor expressed exclusively in the anterior lens epithelium. It is a downstream target of PAX6 and RX and acts as one of the earliest integrators of FGF, BMP, and WNT signaling pathways that cooperate to induce lens formation. In homozygous loss-of-function mutations, complete absence of FOXE3 activity prevents lens placode development during the 4th-5th week of embryogenesis, resulting in primary aphakia. Because the lens serves as an organizer for anterior segment morphogenesis, its absence leads to secondary aplasia of iris, cornea, and anterior chamber structures.

evidence.snippet: expression of FOXE3 restricted to lens tissue, predominantly in the anterior epithelium, suggesting that the extralenticular phenotypes caused by FOXE3 mutations are most likely to be secondary to abnormal lens formation
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that extralenticular phenotypes are secondary to primary lens defects, since FOXE3 expression is restricted to the lens.

evidence.snippet: Approximately 40% of mice heterozygous for Foxe3(dyl) have corneal and lenticular defects
evidence.explanation: Mouse haploinsufficiency model shows secondary corneal defects arising from primary lens abnormalities.

steps/2.description: The lens acts as a critical organizer for anterior segment morphogenesis. In the absence of a lens (aphakia) or with abnormal lens development, secondary malformation of the iris, cornea, and anterior chamber occurs. This explains why FOXE3 mutations, despite the gene being expressed only in the lens, produce extralenticular phenotypes including sclerocornea, Peters anomaly, and iris colobomas.

evidence.snippet: isolated cataract (cerulean type and early onset adult nuclear and cortical cataract)
evidence.explanation: Documents cataract subtypes observed with dominant FOXE3 mutations.

steps/3.description: Lens opacification present at birth or early childhood. In dominant FOXE3 mutations, cataracts can be cerulean type, nuclear, or cortical.

evidence.snippet: Congenital primary aphakia (CPA) is a rare developmental disorder characterized by the absence of lens
evidence.explanation: Defines congenital primary aphakia as the hallmark phenotype of homozygous FOXE3 loss.

steps/4.description: Complete absence of the lens due to failure of lens placode development during the 4th-5th week of embryogenesis. Pathognomonic feature of recessive FOXE3 mutations.

evidence.snippet: we identify new recessive FOXE3 mutations causative for microphthalmia, sclerocornea, primary aphakia, and glaucoma
evidence.explanation: Microphthalmia is a consistent feature of recessive FOXE3 disease.

steps/5.description: Abnormally small eyes, typically bilateral, observed in patients with homozygous FOXE3 mutations as a secondary consequence of failed lens induction.

evidence.snippet: Previous papers have emphasized aphakia and microphthalmia as the primary phenotype, but we find that the initial diagnosis - and perhaps the only one possible in a rural setting - is one of non-syndromic, bilateral, total sclerocornea
evidence.explanation: Highlights sclerocornea as a prominent presenting feature of homozygous FOXE3 mutations.

steps/6.description: Non-inflammatory opacification of the cornea in which the cornea resembles scleral tissue. Total bilateral sclerocornea is a prominent feature of recessive FOXE3 mutations.

evidence.snippet: The phenotype is variable but typically consists of the equivalent of Peters' anomaly in humans, with central corneal opacity, keratolenticular adhesion, and, in some cases, anterior polar cataract
evidence.explanation: Mouse model of Foxe3 haploinsufficiency demonstrates Peters anomaly phenotype.

evidence.snippet: the dominant mutations were penetrant, they gave rise to highly variable phenotypes including iris and chorioretinal colobomas, Peters' anomaly, and isolated cataract
evidence.explanation: Documents Peters anomaly in human patients with heterozygous FOXE3 mutations.

steps/7.description: Central corneal opacity with iridocorneal or keratolenticular adhesions. Associated with heterozygous FOXE3 mutations (dominant) and represents incomplete anterior segment dysgenesis.

evidence.snippet: This original failure leads, in turn, to complete aplasia of the anterior segment of the eye, which is the diagnostic histological criterion for CPA
evidence.explanation: Anterior segment aplasia is the secondary consequence of primary lens failure in FOXE3 disease.

steps/8.description: Broad developmental abnormality of the anterior segment of the eye, which can include iris anomalies, corneal opacities, and lens defects. Represents the overarching phenotypic category.

evidence.snippet: recessive FOXE3 mutations causative for microphthalmia, sclerocornea, primary aphakia, and glaucoma
evidence.explanation: Glaucoma is part of the recessive FOXE3 phenotypic spectrum.

steps/9.description: Elevated intraocular pressure and optic nerve damage, observed as a secondary consequence of anterior segment maldevelopment in recessive FOXE3 disease.

edges/1.description: Absence of the lens leads to secondary malformation of the anterior segment structures.

evidence.snippet: Congenital primary aphakia (CPA) is a rare developmental disorder characterized by the absence of lens
evidence.explanation: Supports congenital aphakia as the direct consequence of failed lens development.

edges/2.description: Early failure of FOXE3-dependent lens development produces congenital primary aphakia.

evidence.snippet: A novel dominant mutation at the stop codon of FOXE3, c.959G>C (p.X320SerextX72), was identified in a patient with congenital cataract
evidence.explanation: Supports congenital cataract as a lens phenotype caused by a FOXE3 mutation.

edges/3.description: Partial or dominant FOXE3 disruption can impair lens differentiation and present as congenital cataract.

evidence.snippet: we identify new recessive FOXE3 mutations causative for microphthalmia, sclerocornea, primary aphakia, and glaucoma
evidence.explanation: Supports microphthalmia as a FOXE3-related anterior segment phenotype.

edges/4.description: Secondary anterior segment dysgenesis from FOXE3 disruption includes microphthalmia.

evidence.snippet: Previous papers have emphasized aphakia and microphthalmia as the primary phenotype, but we find that the initial diagnosis - and perhaps the only one possible in a rural setting - is one of non-syndromic, bilateral, total sclerocornea
evidence.explanation: Supports sclerocornea as a clinical presentation of FOXE3-related anterior segment disease.

edges/5.description: Abnormal lens-dependent anterior segment morphogenesis can present as sclerocornea.

evidence.snippet: the dominant mutations were penetrant, they gave rise to highly variable phenotypes including iris and chorioretinal colobomas, Peters' anomaly, and isolated cataract
evidence.explanation: Supports Peters anomaly as a FOXE3-related phenotype.

edges/6.description: Corneal and lenticular defects from FOXE3 haploinsufficiency can produce Peters anomaly.

evidence.snippet: This original failure leads, in turn, to complete aplasia of the anterior segment of the eye, which is the diagnostic histological criterion for CPA
evidence.explanation: Supports anterior segment aplasia as a downstream effect of primary aphakia.

edges/7.description: Complete lens aplasia secondarily disrupts anterior segment structures.

evidence.snippet: we identify new recessive FOXE3 mutations causative for microphthalmia, sclerocornea, primary aphakia, and glaucoma
evidence.explanation: Supports glaucoma as part of the recessive FOXE3 anterior segment phenotype.

edges/8.description: FOXE3-related anterior segment malformation can include glaucoma.

evidence.snippet: During development Foxe3 is expressed in all undifferentiated lens tissues, and is turned off upon fiber cell differentiation
evidence.explanation: Original discovery that Foxe3 maps to the dysgenetic lens locus and is critical for lens development.

evidence.snippet: Foxe3 had been shown to play a crucial role in vertebrate lens formation and this gene is one of the earliest integrators of several signaling pathways that cooperate to form a lens
evidence.explanation: Review confirming FOXE3 as a central integrator of lens developmental signaling.

evidence.snippet: Functional studies identified variable effects on the protein stability, DNA binding, nuclear localization and transcriptional activity for recessive FOXE3 variants, whereas dominant alleles showed severe impairment in all areas and dominant-negative characteristics.
evidence.explanation: The functional basis for the notes' claim that the dominant alleles behave as dominant negatives rather than by simple haploinsufficiency.

evidence.snippet: Analysis of new and previously reported genetic and clinical data demonstrated a broad phenotypic range with an overlap between recessive and dominant disease.
evidence.explanation: Supports treating the two allele classes as one gene-defined spectrum with overlapping presentations, which is why both subtypes sit in a single entry.

evidence.snippet: FOXE3 | HGNC:3808 | anterior segment dysgenesis | MONDO:0019503 | UD | Moderate
evidence.explanation: ClinGen classifies the FOXE3-anterior segment dysgenesis gene-disease relationship as moderate with undetermined inheritance.

genes/0.notes: FOXE3 encodes a forkhead domain transcription factor expressed exclusively in the lens anterior epithelium during eye development. It is a critical downstream target of PAX6 and RX, and one of the earliest integrators of signaling pathways required for lens formation. The two allele classes are functionally distinct rather than two points on one dosage curve. Dominant alleles are predominantly C-terminal extension variants that append a novel tail past the native stop codon, and in the largest functional survey they were severely impaired in protein stability, DNA binding, nuclear localization and transcriptional activity and behaved as dominant negatives; recessive alleles (truncating and forkhead-domain missense) showed variable effects across the same assays. Heterozygous forkhead-domain missense variants are also reported, so the dominant class is not exclusively extension alleles.

evidence.snippet: We studied a family with hereditary persistent AF and identified the causative mutation (S140G) in the KCNQ1 (KvLQT1) gene on chromosome 11p15.5.
evidence.explanation: Establishes a monogenic atrial-channel variant (KCNQ1 S140G) as the causative lesion in a familial AF kindred.

evidence.snippet: A valine-to-isoleucine mutation at position 93 (V93I) of Kir2.1 was found in all affected members in one kindred.
evidence.explanation: Supports KCNJ2 (Kir2.1) as a second atrial potassium-channel locus carrying a co-segregating variant in a familial AF kindred.

steps/9.description: A germline (or, for GJA5, atrial-tissue-restricted somatic) variant alters an atrial ion channel, a gap-junction protein, or another atrial-restricted protein. The best-characterized variants are gain-of-function in atrial potassium channels (KCNQ1/IKs, KCNJ2/IK1, KCNE2), with additional families carrying GJA5 (connexin 40), NPPA, SCN5A, and loss-of-function KCNA5 (IKur) variants. Three further loci reach this node without a pore-forming potassium or sodium channel being the mutated protein: ABCC9 encodes SUR2A, the regulatory rather than pore-forming subunit of the KATP channel; NUP155 is a nuclear pore component; and MYL4 encodes the atrial-selective essential myosin light chain. The sodium channel beta subunits SCN1B and SCN2B act indirectly, by reducing SCN5A-mediated current.

evidence.snippet: Thus, the S140G mutation is likely to initiate and maintain AF by reducing action potential duration and effective refractory period in atrial myocytes.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports shortened atrial action potential duration and refractory period as the mechanistic link between the gain-of-function channel variant and AF.

evidence.snippet: Functional analysis of the V93I mutant demonstrated a gain-of-function consequence on the Kir2.1 current.
evidence.explanation: Supports increased inward-rectifier current as a second mechanism that shortens atrial repolarization in familial AF.

steps/10.description: Enhanced atrial repolarizing current shortens the atrial action potential duration and effective refractory period. A shorter refractory period reduces the wavelength of atrial reentry, allowing more simultaneous reentrant wavelets to be accommodated within the atria. KCNQ1, KCNE2 and KCNJ2 reach this node by gain of function; KCNA5 does not, and is modelled on the opposite route - loss of IKur lengthens rather than shortens the atrial action potential and produces early afterdepolarizations instead.

evidence.snippet: The cardiac gap-junction protein connexin 40 is expressed selectively in atrial myocytes and mediates the coordinated electrical activation of the atria.
evidence.explanation: Establishes connexin 40 (GJA5) as an atrial-selective gap-junction protein whose dysfunction disrupts coordinated atrial activation.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in GJA5 may predispose patients to idiopathic atrial fibrillation by impairing gap-junction assembly or electrical coupling.
evidence.explanation: Supports impaired gap-junction coupling as the mechanism by which GJA5 variants predispose the atria to fibrillation.

steps/11.description: In GJA5-related familial AF, variants in connexin 40 impair gap-junction assembly and intercellular electrical coupling between atrial myocytes, producing heterogeneous, slowed atrial conduction that promotes reentry. This is a coupling/conduction mechanism that converges on the same arrhythmogenic substrate as the channelopathy arm.

evidence.snippet: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a common cardiac arrhythmia whose molecular etiology is poorly understood.
evidence.explanation: Frames the clinical endpoint (atrial fibrillation) whose monogenic molecular etiology this entry models.

steps/12.description: Shortened refractoriness and/or impaired coupling create an atrial substrate that supports multiple coexisting reentrant wavelets and ectopic triggers, initiating and maintaining atrial fibrillation. As AF persists, electrical remodeling further shortens refractoriness ("AF begets AF").

evidence.snippet: We studied a family with hereditary persistent AF and identified the causative mutation (S140G) in the KCNQ1 (KvLQT1) gene on chromosome 11p15.5.
evidence.explanation: Documents persistent atrial fibrillation as the segregating clinical phenotype in a familial AF kindred.

steps/13.description: The clinical manifestation: paroxysmal, persistent, or permanent atrial fibrillation, typically with earlier onset than acquired AF and often in structurally normal hearts. Loss of organized atrial contraction predisposes to thromboembolism and stroke.

edges/13.description: Gain-of-function potassium-channel variants increase repolarizing current and abbreviate the atrial action potential duration and effective refractory period.

edges/14.description: A shortened refractory period and reduced reentry wavelength establish a substrate permissive for sustained reentrant atrial activity.

edges/15.description: Impaired electrical coupling slows and disorganizes atrial conduction, contributing to the reentrant substrate.

edges/16.description: The reentry-prone atrial substrate manifests clinically as sustained or recurrent atrial fibrillation.

evidence.snippet: We studied a family with hereditary persistent AF and identified the causative mutation (S140G) in the KCNQ1 (KvLQT1) gene on chromosome 11p15.5.
evidence.explanation: Establishes S140G as the causative mutation in a family with hereditary persistent AF, which is the human genetic basis for listing KCNQ1 as a causative gene here.

evidence.snippet: Functional analysis of the S140G mutant revealed a gain-of-function effect on the KCNQ1/KCNE1 and the KCNQ1/KCNE2 currents, which contrasts with the dominant negative or loss-of-function effects of the KCNQ1 mutations previously identified in patients with long QT syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the gain-of-function direction, distinct from the loss-of-function KCNQ1 mechanism of long QT syndrome. Graded IN_VITRO because the measurement is heterologous-expression electrophysiology in COS cells rather than a human observation.

evidence.snippet: Kir2.1 V93I mutation may play a role in initiating and/or maintaining AF by increasing the activity of the inward rectifier K(+) channel.
evidence.explanation: Supports KCNJ2 gain-of-function as a causative familial-AF mechanism via increased IK1.

evidence.snippet: Four novel heterozygous missense mutations were identified in 4 of the 15 patients.
evidence.explanation: Documents GJA5 missense variants (somatic and germline) in patients with idiopathic AF.

evidence.snippet: The mutation was present in all affected members in the two kindreds and was absent in 462 healthy unrelated Chinese subjects.
evidence.explanation: Cosegregation in two kindreds with absence from a large control set, the human-genetic basis of the KCNE2 claim.

evidence.snippet: An arginine-to-cysteine mutation at position 27 (R27C) of KCNE2, the beta subunit of the KCNQ1-KCNE2 channel responsible for a background potassium current, was found in 2 of the 28 probands.
evidence.explanation: The variant and the 2-of-28 yield quoted in this record's note.

evidence.snippet: Similar to KCNQ1 S140G, the mutation had a gain-of-function effect on the KCNQ1-KCNE2 channel; unlike long QT syndrome-associated KCNE2 mutations, it did not alter HERG-KCNE2 current.
evidence.explanation: Functional demonstration that the AF-associated KCNE2 variant acts by gain of function, and distinguishes it from the long-QT KCNE2 mechanism.

genes/3.notes: The reported lesion is a single recurrent substitution, R27C, found in 2 of 28 unrelated Chinese AF kindreds, cosegregating with disease in both and absent from 462 controls. Its functional effect parallels KCNQ1 S140G - a gain of function on the KCNQ1-KCNE2 channel - which is why the two are modelled on the same repolarization-shortening arm of this entry.

evidence.snippet: In a family with 11 clinically affected members, we mapped an atrial fibrillation locus to chromosome 1p36-p35 and identified a heterozygous frameshift mutation in the gene encoding atrial natriuretic peptide.
evidence.explanation: The linkage and variant identification behind the NPPA claim, with the size of the informative family.

evidence.snippet: Circulating chimeric atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) was detected in high concentration in subjects with the mutation
evidence.explanation: The human half of the mechanism: carriers of the frameshift circulate the chimeric peptide at high concentration, which is what makes the peptide rather than loss of normal ANP the candidate mediator.

evidence.snippet: shortened atrial action potentials were seen in an isolated heart model, creating a possible substrate for atrial fibrillation
evidence.explanation: Links the NPPA frameshift to atrial action potential shortening, the mechanism this entry models; the electrophysiology is from isolated perfused rat heart rather than from patients, so this half is graded MODEL_ORGANISM.

genes/4.notes: NPPA is the one locus in this entry whose product is a circulating hormone rather than an ion channel or a junctional protein. The defining family was mapped by linkage to 1p36-p35 and carries a heterozygous frameshift; the mutant peptide circulates at high concentration and shortens the atrial action potential, which is how the entry connects it to the shared re-entry-prone substrate.

evidence.snippet: In 10 probands (2.7%), 8 novel variants not found in the control population (0%; P=0.001) were identified.
evidence.explanation: The yield of novel SCN5A variants in a resequenced AF cohort against matched controls.

evidence.snippet: Mutations or rare variants in SCN5A may predispose patients with or without underlying heart disease to AF.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own hedged conclusion, and the reason this record is graded as a risk factor rather than as causative.

evidence.snippet: We also identified 11 rare missense variants in 12 probands (3.2%) that have previously been associated with inherited arrhythmia syndromes (eg, congenital long-QT syndrome and Brugada syndrome).
evidence.explanation: The overlap with long-QT and Brugada variants quoted in this record's note, at a share comparable to the novel-variant yield above it.

genes/5.notes: Graded RISK_FACTOR rather than CAUSATIVE deliberately. The largest resequencing study found novel variants in 2.7% of AF probands with cosegregation in six informative families, but its own conclusion is that such variants "may predispose" to AF, and a further 3.2% of probands carried rare variants already attributed to long-QT or Brugada syndrome. SCN5A is therefore better read as a shared arrhythmia-susceptibility locus whose AF phenotype overlaps other sodium-channel syndromes than as a dedicated familial-AF gene.

evidence.snippet: The heterozygous E375X mutation, present in a familial case of atrial fibrillation and absent in 540 unrelated control individuals, introduced a premature stop codon disrupting the Kv1.5 channel protein.
evidence.explanation: The human variant and its absence from controls, the genetic basis of the KCNA5 claim.

evidence.snippet: Genomic DNA scanning revealed a nonsense mutation in KCNA5 that encodes Kv1.5, a voltage-gated potassium channel expressed in human atria.
evidence.explanation: Source for the atrial expression of Kv1.5 recorded in this record's note.

evidence.snippet: Loss of channel function translated into action potential prolongation and early after-depolarization in human atrial myocytes, increasing vulnerability to stress-provoked triggered activity.
evidence.explanation: The mechanism recorded in the note above: IKur loss lengthens rather than shortens the atrial action potential.

genes/6.notes:
KCNA5 runs opposite to the potassium-channel subtypes above: KCNQ1, KCNE2 and KCNJ2 act by gain of function and shorten the atrial action potential, whereas KCNA5 loss of IKur prolongs it and produces early afterdepolarization and triggered activity. Both routes converge on an arrhythmogenic atrium, which is worth keeping visible because it means action potential shortening is not a necessary feature of monogenic AF.
The channel is described by its discoverers as expressed in human atria, which is the reason a defect in it produces an atrial arrhythmia.

evidence.snippet: K(ATP) channelopathy caused by missense mutation (Thr1547Ile) of the ABCC9 gene conferring predisposition to adrenergic AF originating from the vein of Marshall.
evidence.explanation: The diagnosis line of the single case report that is the whole human basis of the ABCC9 claim.

evidence.snippet: A 53-year-old female presented with a 10-year history of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (AF), precipitated by activity and refractory to medical therapy.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the report concerns one patient, which is the reason for the UNKNOWN grading.

genes/7.notes:
Graded UNKNOWN rather than CAUSATIVE because the human evidence is a single proband. The report is a clinical case with supporting molecular phenotyping and a targeted knockout, not a family with segregation, and no independent AF family was found when PubMed was searched for ABCC9 with atrial fibrillation, and for SUR2A with KATP channel and atrial fibrillation, in September 2026: those searches returned this case report and reviews citing it, and no independent family series. MONDO nevertheless lists the gene as the causal gene of atrial fibrillation, familial, 12, which is what this record reconciles against; the disagreement is about strength of evidence rather than about whether the observation exists.
No inheritance block is recorded here on purpose: a single proband does not establish a mode of inheritance.

evidence.snippet: We identified 2 nonsynonymous variants in SCN1B (resulting in R85H, D153N) and 2 in SCN2B (R28Q, R28W) in patients with AF.
evidence.explanation: The variant identification behind both the SCN1B and the SCN2B records.

evidence.snippet: Screening for mutations in the 4 beta-subunit genes was performed in 480 patients with AF (118 patients with lone AF and 362 patients with AF and cardiovascular disease) and 548 control subjects (188 ethnically defined anonymized subjects and 360 subjects without AF).
evidence.explanation: The screen and its denominators, quoted in this record's note.

evidence.snippet: In 3 of 4 mutation carriers, the ECGs showed saddleback-type ST-segment elevation in the right precordial leads.
evidence.explanation: The Brugada-overlap electrocardiographic phenotype recorded in the note.

genes/8.notes:
SCN1B and SCN2B were reported together in one screen of 480 AF patients against 548 controls. The variants are rare, at conserved residues, absent from controls, and reduce sodium current in heterologous expression - but the report describes probands rather than pedigrees, so cosegregation is not established and the grading here is UNKNOWN.
A detail worth carrying: three of the four beta-subunit variant carriers had saddleback right-precordial ST elevation, which places these variants in the Brugada-overlap part of the sodium-channel spectrum rather than in isolated AF.

evidence.snippet: We identified 2 nonsynonymous variants in SCN1B (resulting in R85H, D153N) and 2 in SCN2B (R28Q, R28W) in patients with AF.
evidence.explanation: The variant identification behind this record.

evidence.snippet: In heterologous expression studies using Chinese hamster ovary cells, the mutant beta1- or beta2-subunits reduced SCN5A-mediated current and altered channel gating compared with coexpression of wild-type subunits.
evidence.explanation: The functional effect shared by the SCN1B and SCN2B variants: reduced sodium current through the Nav1.5 alpha subunit.

genes/9.notes: From the same screen as SCN1B above and graded the same way, for the same reason: probands rather than pedigrees. The functional direction is shared with SCN5A loss of function, which is the mechanistic argument the authors make for a sodium-current route to AF.

evidence.snippet: We have identified a homozygous mutation, R391H, in NUP155 that cosegregates with AF, affects nuclear localization of NUP155, and reduces nuclear envelope permeability.
evidence.explanation: Cosegregation of a homozygous NUP155 variant with AF, plus its cell biological effect.

evidence.snippet: Homozygous NUP155(-/-) knockout mice die before E8.5, but heterozygous NUP155(+/-) mice show the AF phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Model-organism support that reduced NUP155 dosage is sufficient for an AF phenotype.

evidence.snippet: The R391H mutation and reduction of NUP155 are associated with inhibition of both export of Hsp70 mRNA and nuclear import of Hsp70 protein.
evidence.explanation: The specific transport defect named in this record's note.

genes/10.notes: The only nuclear pore gene in this entry, and the one whose mechanism is furthest from ion flux: the reported defect is in nucleocytoplasmic transport, specifically of Hsp70 message and protein. It is also the strongest of the newer loci on human-plus-model evidence, since the heterozygous knockout mouse reproduces the AF phenotype even though the human variant is homozygous.

evidence.snippet: We found eight homozygous carriers of the mutation, all of whom had early-onset AF.
evidence.explanation: The homozygote count and the complete penetrance among them.

evidence.snippet: We discovered a rare frameshift deletion in the myosin MYL4 gene (c.234delC) that associates with early-onset AF under a recessive mode of inheritance (allelic frequency = 0.58%).
evidence.explanation: The variant, its frequency, and the recessive mode of inheritance recorded above.

evidence.snippet: Through a population approach we found a loss of function mutation in the myosin gene MYL4 that, in the homozygous state, is completely penetrant for early-onset AF.
evidence.explanation: The penetrance claim and the population-based study design.

evidence.snippet: Three of the homozygotes had received pacemaker implantations due to sick sinus syndrome, three had suffered an ischemic stroke, and one suffered sudden cardiac death.
evidence.explanation: The sick sinus syndrome, stroke and sudden death recorded in this record's note as the wider atrial-cardiomyopathy phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Myosin light-chain 4 (MYL4), encoding the atrial-selective essential myosin light chain, was identified as a candidate gene.
evidence.explanation: Source for describing MYL4's product as the atrial-selective essential myosin light chain.

evidence.snippet: The mutation cosegregated with atrial standstill (selected as the principal presenting trait) with a logarithm of the odds score of 5.3.
evidence.explanation: The independent family and cosegregation supporting MYL4 beyond the Icelandic population study.

evidence.snippet: Both MYL4 p.E11K knock-in rats and MYL4 knockout rats showed progressive atrial electrophysiological, contractile, and fibrotic abnormalities, similar to affected patients.
evidence.explanation: Model-organism support for the atrial cardiomyopathy phenotype recorded in this record's note.

genes/11.notes:
MYL4 is the clearest demonstration in this entry that a monogenic AF gene need not be a channel: the product is the atrial-selective essential myosin light chain, and the phenotype is an atrial cardiomyopathy that includes sick sinus syndrome, stroke and sudden death alongside the arrhythmia. An independent family, reported separately, cosegregated a different MYL4 missense variant with atrial standstill, and knock-in and knockout rats reproduced the progressive electrical, contractile and fibrotic phenotype.
It is also the only locus here found by a population approach rather than by following a family, which is why the penetrance statement is unusually strong for this list. No case fraction is recorded: the study reports the allelic frequency and a homozygote count rather than a share of cases, and computing one from those two numbers would not be a reported figure.

evidence.snippet: A variant in the ZFHX3 gene on chromosome 16q22, rs7193343-T, associated significantly with AF (odds ratio OR = 1.21, P = 1.4 x 10(-10)).
evidence.explanation: The association and its effect size, which is the basis for grading this locus SUSCEPTIBILITY rather than causative.

genes/12.notes:
This record exists to reconcile a MONDO assertion this entry disagrees with. MONDO relates atrial fibrillation, familial, 8 to ZFHX3 with RO:0004003, "has material basis in germline mutation in" - the same relation it uses for KCNQ1 and MYL4. The underlying finding is not of that kind. It is a genome-wide association signal at a common intronic variant with an odds ratio of about 1.2, discovered in 2,385 cases and 33,752 controls and replicated in Norwegian and US samples; no rare coding variant, no family, and no segregation is reported.
Three further features mark it as a common-variant locus rather than a Mendelian one. The risk allele did not reach significance in a Han Chinese cohort, where it is also far more common (control frequency 0.68 against 0.14-0.20 in the European samples). The same variant associates with ischaemic and cardioembolic stroke, as a downstream consequence of AF. And the authors found no association between the variant and ZFHX3 expression in the tissues they tested, so even the gene assignment within the locus is by proximity rather than by demonstrated effect.
It is retained, and bound, because the association itself is solid: it was replicated in two independent non-Icelandic samples in the original report, and in the same study only the previously known 4q25/PITX2 signal was more significant. What is wrong is the relation, not the fact.

evidence.snippet: GM1 gangliosidosis is a progressive, neurosomatic, lysosomal storage disorder caused by mutations in the GLB1 gene encoding the enzyme β-galactosidase.
evidence.explanation: GLB1 mutations cause GM1 gangliosidosis; partial activity yields the late-infantile/juvenile form.

evidence.snippet: Beyond palliative and supportive care, no FDA-approved treatments exist for GM1 patients.
evidence.explanation: Care is supportive in the absence of approved disease-modifying therapy.

treatments/0.description: No FDA-approved disease-modifying therapy exists; management is supportive, including seizure control and rehabilitation.

evidence.snippet: We found that pathogenic missense variants in transmembrane and linker domains (misTMD+Linker) were associated with severe developmental phenotypes
evidence.explanation: Identifies transmembrane/linker missense variants as the genotype class underlying the severe developmental phenotype.

evidence.snippet: This mutation resulted in a leucine to methionine substitution (NP_000824.1:p.L812M) in the linker region connecting the ligand-binding domain to the pore-forming transmembrane region of GluN2A
evidence.explanation: Localizes the p.L812M early-onset epileptic encephalopathy variant to the ligand-binding-domain-to-transmembrane linker.

evidence.snippet: Notably, this was paralleled by electrophysiology data, where misTMD+Linker predominantly led to NMDAR gain-of-function, while misATD+LBD exclusively caused NMDAR loss-of-function.
evidence.explanation: Electrophysiological classification of GRIN2A allele classes by domain.

steps/1.description: A heterozygous, typically de novo, GRIN2A missense variant falling in the transmembrane domains or the linkers that couple the ligand-binding domain to the channel (misTMD+Linker) alters the GluN2A subunit within the gating and ion-permeation machinery of the NMDA receptor. Recurrent examples include p.Leu812Met in the S2-M4 linker, p.Asn615Lys and p.Asn615Ser in the pore-lining M2 reentrant loop, and p.Ser644Gly. This variant class is the genetic entry point for the severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy end of the GRIN2A spectrum.

evidence.snippet: misATD+LBD exclusively caused NMDAR loss-of-function
evidence.explanation: Assigns amino-terminal/ligand-binding-domain missense variants to the loss-of-function class.

evidence.snippet: With respect to null variants, we show that Grin2a+/- cortical rat neurons also had reduced NMDAR function and there was no evidence of previously postulated compensatory overexpression of GluN2B.
evidence.explanation: Shows null variants also reduce NMDA-receptor function, without GluN2B compensation.

evidence.snippet: Two pathogenic de novo GRIN2A null variants were identified in patients with ABPE who had less severe ID, despite the electrical status epilepticus during slow-wave sleep (ESES).
evidence.explanation: An independent cohort assembled at the severe end of the epilepsy-aphasia spectrum found null variants in the patients with the LESS severe intellectual disability, corroborating that this genotype class does not produce the severe developmental phenotype curated in this entry.

evidence.snippet: Of these mutations, 9 (31.0%) are situated in amino (N)-terminal domain, 6 (20.7%) in linger-binding domain S1, and 10 (34.5%) in linger-binding domain S2.
evidence.explanation: A literature-wide tally of GRIN2A loss-of-function variants places the large majority in the amino-terminal and ligand-binding domains, independently corroborating the domain localization assigned to this genotype class. (The source misspells "ligand-binding" as "linger-binding"; the snippet reproduces the published text verbatim.)

evidence.snippet: Notably, this was paralleled by electrophysiology data, where misTMD+Linker predominantly led to NMDAR gain-of-function, while misATD+LBD exclusively caused NMDAR loss-of-function.
evidence.explanation: Electrophysiological classification of GRIN2A allele classes by domain.

steps/2.description: The alternative genotype class: GRIN2A null variants (nonsense, frameshift, splice, exon-disrupting deletions) and missense variants confined to the amino-terminal or ligand-binding domains (misATD+LBD). These act through loss of receptor function. This class predominantly produces the milder GRIN2A epilepsy-aphasia phenotypes curated separately (self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes, Landau-Kleffner syndrome), and is included here because a minority of individuals at the severe developmental end carry loss-of-function variants and because this class defines eligibility for co-agonist (L-serine) therapy.

evidence.snippet: We observed that the GluN2A P1199Rfs*32-containing receptors traffic efficiently to the postsynaptic membrane but have increased extra-synaptic expression relative to WT GluN2A-containing NMDARs.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the mistargeting phenotype: trafficking to the membrane is preserved but synaptic localization is lost.

evidence.snippet: Indeed, we observed impaired binding to the scaffolding protein postsynaptic protein-95 (PSD-95); however, we found the mutant interacts with Scribble1, which facilitates the recycling of both the mutant and the WT GluN2A.
evidence.explanation: Identifies loss of PSD-95 binding with retained Scribble1 recycling as the molecular basis of the mislocalization.

steps/3.description: A mechanistically distinct third route to reduced GluN2A function, separate from gene-dosage loss and from impaired agonist binding: a frameshift truncating the GluN2A intracellular C-terminal domain leaves the receptor able to reach the postsynaptic membrane but destroys its PDZ interaction with the scaffolding protein PSD-95, so the receptor is mislocalized to extrasynaptic membrane while retaining Scribble1-mediated recycling. The consequence is fewer synapses and reduced dendritic spine density. This is a trafficking and localization defect rather than a channel-gating defect, and it was identified in a patient with epileptic encephalopathy, multiple seizure types, and severe aphasia.

evidence.snippet: A de novo GRIN2A missense mutation (c.2434C>A; p.L812M) increased the charge transfer mediated by NMDA receptors containing the mutant GluN2A-L812M subunit.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates increased NMDA-receptor charge transfer for a linker-domain variant causing early-onset epileptic encephalopathy.

evidence.snippet: These data support the idea that GluN2A-L812M-containing NMDARs are overactive due to the increased activation at low concentrations of agonists.
evidence.explanation: Increased agonist potency is one biophysical route to receptor overactivity.

evidence.snippet: receptor currents revealed a loss of the Mg²(+) block and a decrease in Ca²(+) permeability
evidence.explanation: The pore-loop p.N615K variant abolishes the magnesium block while reducing calcium permeability, the mixed biophysical signature noted above.

evidence.snippet: In heterologous cells, mutant receptors had enhanced NMDA receptor agonist potency and slow deactivation following rapid removal of glutamate, as occurs at synapses.
evidence.explanation: Adds slowed deactivation as a second gain-of-function route, for the p.Ser644Gly developmental and epileptic encephalopathy variant.

steps/4.description: Transmembrane and linker missense variants increase NMDA-receptor function by several convergent biophysical routes: increased agonist (glutamate and glycine) potency, slowed deactivation after synaptic glutamate is cleared, and loss of the voltage-dependent extracellular magnesium block of the channel pore, which renders receptor calcium signaling voltage-independent. The net effect is greater charge transfer per receptor activation. Notably, pore-loop variants can simultaneously reduce calcium permeability while abolishing magnesium block, so gain-of-function here denotes increased overall charge transfer and excitatory drive rather than a uniform increase in every biophysical parameter.

evidence.snippet: Grin2a+/- cortical rat neurons also had reduced NMDAR function
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates reduced NMDA-receptor function with GRIN2A haploinsufficiency.

evidence.snippet: Pathogenic missense variants in GRIN2A and GRIN2B may result in gain or loss of function (GoF/LoF) of the N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR).
evidence.explanation: Establishes the two-functional-class model that this node's loss-of-function arm represents.

steps/5.description: Null variants and amino-terminal or ligand-binding-domain missense variants reduce NMDA-receptor-mediated current, through haploinsufficiency of GluN2A or impaired agonist binding, without compensatory upregulation of GluN2B. Because GluN2A-containing receptors carry much of the mature excitatory synaptic NMDA current, this too dysregulates developmentally tuned NMDA-receptor signaling, but it characteristically produces the milder epilepsy-aphasia end of the spectrum rather than this severe entity.

evidence.snippet: The resulting enhanced excitatory drive is consistent with the production of an epileptic phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Links increased receptor activity to enhanced excitatory drive and epilepsy.

evidence.snippet: The NMDA receptor-mediated Ca2+ signaling during simultaneous pre- and postsynaptic activity is critically involved in synaptic plasticity and thus has a key role in the nervous system.
evidence.explanation: Establishes coincidence-dependent NMDA-receptor calcium signaling as the function that magnesium-block loss subverts.

steps/6.description: The immediate cellular consequence of gain-of-function receptors is enhanced NMDA-receptor-mediated cation flux, with excessive depolarizing charge transfer and excessive calcium entry, at synapses that are simultaneously less able to terminate the signal (slow deactivation) and less protected by magnesium block at resting potential. Because calcium entry through NMDA receptors during coincident pre- and postsynaptic activity is the principal instructive signal for activity-dependent synaptic refinement, the excess is both an excitatory and a developmental-signaling insult, and the loss of its voltage dependence destroys the coincidence detection the signal depends on.

evidence.snippet: Our findings suggest that disturbances in the neuronal electrophysiological balance during development result in variable neurological phenotypes depending on which NR2 subunit of NMDA receptors is affected.
evidence.explanation: Frames the disorder as a developmental disturbance of neuronal electrophysiological balance.

evidence.snippet: In GRIN2-variant patients alterations of this coincidence detection provoked complex clinical phenotypes, ranging from reduced muscle strength to epileptic seizures and intellectual disability.
evidence.explanation: Connects disrupted NMDA-receptor coincidence detection to the clinical spectrum of seizures and intellectual disability. The cited publication is a mouse study, hence MODEL_ORGANISM; this particular sentence is the paper's framing of the human phenotype context rather than its own primary data, and the paper's own experimental findings are cited separately elsewhere in this entry.

steps/7.description: The convergence point of both functional classes: NMDA-receptor-mediated glutamatergic signaling and its calcium-dependent downstream cascades fall outside the narrow range that the developing cortex requires. Because GluN2A expression rises through late infancy and childhood as GluN2B-containing receptors are replaced, the perturbation lands on a moving developmental target, which is one reason the same gene produces phenotypes ranging from isolated speech apraxia to a lethal encephalopathy.

evidence.snippet: Multielectrode recordings of neuronal networks revealed hyperexcitability and altered bursting and synchronicity.
evidence.explanation: Directly demonstrates network hyperexcitability and altered synchronicity in a GRIN2A developmental and epileptic encephalopathy knock-in model.

evidence.snippet: all homozygotes exhibited lethal tonic-clonic seizures by mid-third week
evidence.explanation: The knock-in model develops spontaneous, ultimately lethal seizures, confirming the epileptogenic consequence.

evidence.snippet: we show that voltage-independent glutamate-gated signaling of GluN2A-containing NMDA receptors is associated with NMDAR-dependent audiogenic seizures due to hyperexcitable midbrain circuits
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates hyperexcitability with a specific regional locus (midbrain), supporting but regionally qualifying the excitation-inhibition imbalance claim.

steps/8.description: Dysregulated NMDA-receptor signaling shifts the balance between excitation and inhibition in developing cortical, hippocampal, and midbrain networks, producing neuronal hyperexcitability with abnormal bursting and abnormal network synchronicity. This is the substrate of the multiple early-onset, predominantly drug-resistant focal and generalized seizure types that define the epileptic component of the encephalopathy. The shift is not uniform across regions: in gain-of-function models midbrain circuits become hyperexcitable while hippocampal oscillatory activity is reduced.

evidence.snippet: Homozygous and heterozygous mutant mice exhibited altered hippocampal morphology at 2 weeks of age
evidence.explanation: Structural hippocampal abnormality in the knock-in model at an early developmental stage supports impaired synaptic and circuit maturation.

evidence.snippet: GRIN2A-related disorders encompass a broad phenotypic spectrum that includes developmental delay evolving to intellectual disability (DD/ID), epilepsy, speech and language disorders, movement disorders, and neuropsychiatric disorders.
evidence.explanation: Developmental delay, intellectual disability, and speech-language disorder are the clinical output of impaired synaptic maturation.

steps/9.description: NMDA-receptor calcium signaling is the instructive signal for activity-dependent synapse formation, pruning, and long-term potentiation and depression. Dysregulation on either side of the optimum disrupts dendritic and synaptic maturation and produces altered hippocampal morphology, providing the substrate for global developmental delay, intellectual disability, and the prominent speech and language impairment of GRIN2A-related disorders.

evidence.snippet: Neuroimaging revealed widespread cerebral parenchymal volume loss, a thin corpus callosum, and abnormal myelination of the terminal zones and temporal lobes bilaterally.
evidence.explanation: Documents the characteristic MRI signature of the severe GRIN2A phenotype.

evidence.snippet: These findings reflected progression compared to previous studies.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the volume loss is progressive on serial imaging.

steps/10.description: Serial brain MRI in the severe GRIN2A phenotype shows widespread and progressive cerebral parenchymal volume loss with a thin corpus callosum and abnormal myelination of the terminal zones and temporal lobes, while the cerebellum and brainstem are relatively spared. This progressive structural loss distinguishes the severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy from the structurally subtle perisylvian and hippocampal changes described in the GRIN2A epilepsy-aphasia phenotypes, and it is the anatomical correlate of the static, profoundly impaired developmental trajectory. Whether it is driven by receptor-mediated excitotoxicity, by the seizure burden, or by an independent process is unresolved.

evidence.snippet: Epilepsy is typically focal and ranges from self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes to developmental and/or epileptic encephalopathies (DEE/EE)
evidence.explanation: Places developmental and epileptic encephalopathy at the severe end of the GRIN2A epilepsy spectrum.

evidence.snippet: other GluN2A mutations extend the range of phenotypes beyond disorders in the epilepsy-aphasia spectrum to include early-onset epileptic encephalopathy, which is characterized by severe infantile-onset epilepsy and lack of development.
evidence.explanation: Defines the entity as distinct from, and more severe than, the epilepsy-aphasia spectrum phenotypes.

steps/11.description: The defining phenotype: an early-onset epileptic encephalopathy in which frequent seizures and abundant epileptiform activity compound an independently abnormal developmental trajectory. Within the GRIN2A spectrum this sits at the opposite pole from self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes.

evidence.snippet: Intellect ranges from normal to profoundly impaired.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews documents the range of intellectual outcome, of which this entity occupies the impaired end.

evidence.snippet: early-onset epileptic encephalopathy associated with profound cognitive impairment, absent motor development, and intractable seizures
evidence.explanation: The index severe case had profound cognitive impairment.

steps/12.description: Intellectual disability that in this severe subgroup ranges from moderate to profound; across the wider GRIN2A spectrum intellect ranges from normal to profoundly impaired.

evidence.snippet: developmental delay evolving to intellectual disability (DD/ID)
evidence.explanation: Developmental delay evolving to intellectual disability is a core feature.

evidence.snippet: Development was static at a neonatal level without further progression or regression.
evidence.explanation: Illustrates the profound, static developmental impairment at the severe end.

steps/13.description: Global developmental delay is present from infancy and evolves into intellectual disability. In the most severe cases development is static at a neonatal level rather than regressive.

evidence.snippet: Epilepsy is typically focal
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews states that GRIN2A-related epilepsy is typically focal.

evidence.snippet: Standard anti-epileptic drug monotherapy was ineffective in the patient.
evidence.explanation: Documents drug resistance in the index GRIN2A developmental and epileptic encephalopathy patient.

steps/14.description: GRIN2A-related epilepsy is typically focal. At the severe end seizures begin in infancy or early childhood and are usually refractory to multiple anti-seizure medications.

evidence.snippet: Seizures evolved to involve tonic flexion or extension of all extremities lasting minutes
evidence.explanation: Describes the tonic seizure semiology in the severe phenotype.

steps/15.description: Tonic seizures with flexion or extension of all extremities, lasting seconds to minutes, occurring at up to near-daily frequency.

evidence.snippet: the myoclonic jerks continuing to occur alone or in association with these larger seizures

evidence.snippet: The child exhibited frequent random multifocal myoclonic movements of his extremities.

steps/16.description: Frequent myoclonic jerks, occurring alone or as the initiating event of larger tonic seizures, together with near-continuous random multifocal myoclonic movements of the extremities.

evidence.snippet: EEGs were reported to possess a diffusely slow and disorganized background with irregularly generalized or lateralized runs of spike and slow wave discharges

evidence.explanation: Distinguishes the severe phenotype's EEG from the sleep-activated (ESES/CSWS) pattern of the GRIN2A epilepsy-aphasia phenotypes.

steps/17.description: EEG shows a diffusely slow, disorganized background with irregular generalized or lateralized runs of spike-and-slow-wave discharges, in the index severe case frontally predominant and greater on the right. Notably, in the severe phenotype the discharges need not be sleep-activated: unlike the GRIN2A epilepsy-aphasia phenotypes, features of electrical status epilepticus in sleep may be absent entirely.

evidence.snippet: abnormal with slow activity of 3.5-4.5 hertz and 1-3 hertz delta and disorganized activity
evidence.explanation: Documents the diffusely slow, disorganized EEG background.

steps/18.description: A diffusely slow, poorly organized waking background with delta activity, reflecting the encephalopathic state independent of individual seizures.

evidence.snippet: Neuroimaging revealed widespread cerebral parenchymal volume loss
evidence.explanation: Documents cerebral parenchymal volume loss.

evidence.snippet: These findings reflected progression compared to previous studies.
evidence.explanation: Confirms the atrophy is progressive.

steps/19.description: Widespread cerebral parenchymal volume loss that progresses on serial MRI, with relative sparing of cerebellum and brainstem.

evidence.snippet: widespread cerebral parenchymal volume loss, a thin corpus callosum
evidence.explanation: Documents the thin corpus callosum.

steps/20.description: A thin corpus callosum accompanies the cerebral volume loss and is part of the MRI signature named in the disorder's clinical definition.

evidence.snippet: abnormal myelination of the terminal zones and temporal lobes bilaterally
evidence.explanation: Documents the abnormal cerebral myelination.

steps/21.description: Abnormal myelination affecting the terminal zones and temporal lobes bilaterally, on a background of cerebral volume loss.

evidence.snippet: Observed speech disorders include dysarthria and speech dyspraxia, and both receptive and expressive language delays
evidence.explanation: Establishes the prominent expressive and receptive speech-language impairment of GRIN2A-related disorders; absence of speech at the severe end follows from, but is not stated by, this spectrum-level description, hence the indirect marking.

evidence.snippet: Development was static at a neonatal level without further progression or regression.
evidence.explanation: The index severe case remained developmentally at a neonatal level and so never acquired expressive speech; the paper does not state the absence in so many words, hence the indirect marking.

steps/22.description: Speech and language impairment is the signature of GRIN2A-related disorders, ranging from subtly reduced conversational intelligibility to dysarthria and speech dyspraxia; at this severe end expressive speech may be entirely absent.

evidence.snippet: profound cognitive impairment, absent motor development, and intractable seizures
evidence.explanation: Documents absent motor development at the severe end.

steps/23.description: Gross and fine motor development is delayed and, in the most severely affected, purposeful motor development is absent.

evidence.snippet: misTMD+Linker predominantly led to NMDAR gain-of-function
evidence.explanation: Electrophysiology links this variant class to gain-of-function.

edges/3.description: Variants in the gating and permeation machinery predominantly increase receptor function.

evidence.snippet: misATD+LBD exclusively caused NMDAR loss-of-function
evidence.explanation: Electrophysiology assigns this variant class to loss-of-function.

edges/4.description: Haploinsufficiency or impaired agonist binding reduces receptor function.

evidence.snippet: Overall, our data show that GluN2A P1199Rfs*32 is a loss-of-function variant with altered membrane localization in neurons
evidence.explanation: The authors classify the trafficking defect as loss-of-function.

edges/5.description: Extrasynaptic mislocalization removes GluN2A from the synapse, producing net loss of synaptic NMDA-receptor function.

evidence.snippet: we found that neurons expressing GluN2A P1199Rfs*32 have fewer synapses and decreased spine density, indicating compromised synaptic transmission in these neurons
evidence.explanation: Measures the structural synaptic consequence directly in neurons.

edges/6.description: Mislocalized receptors leave neurons with fewer synapses and lower spine density, a direct structural hit to synaptic maturation that does not require passing through altered channel gating.

evidence.snippet: increased the charge transfer mediated by NMDA receptors containing the mutant GluN2A-L812M subunit
evidence.explanation: Directly measures increased charge transfer as the consequence of the gain-of-function variant.

edges/7.description: Increased agonist potency, slowed deactivation, and loss of magnesium block all increase current flow through the receptor.

evidence.snippet: Grin2a+/- cortical rat neurons also had reduced NMDAR function
evidence.explanation: Reduced NMDA-receptor function in Grin2a-haploinsufficient neurons is the perturbation this edge carries forward.

edges/8.description: Reduced receptor function also perturbs developmentally tuned NMDA-receptor signaling, but with a characteristically milder developmental phenotype.

evidence.snippet: The resulting enhanced excitatory drive is consistent with the production of an epileptic phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Enhanced excitatory drive is the dysregulated-signaling state this edge produces.

edges/9.description: Excess and voltage-independent charge transfer is the gain-of-function route into dysregulated NMDA-receptor signaling.

evidence.snippet: Multielectrode recordings of neuronal networks revealed hyperexcitability and altered bursting and synchronicity.
evidence.explanation: Network hyperexcitability is measured directly downstream of the dysregulated receptor in a patient-variant knock-in model.

edges/10.description: Dysregulated NMDA-receptor signaling shifts cortical network excitability.

evidence.snippet: The NMDA receptor-mediated Ca2+ signaling during simultaneous pre- and postsynaptic activity is critically involved in synaptic plasticity
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the dysregulated signal is the one that instructs synaptic plasticity.

edges/11.description: NMDA-receptor calcium signaling instructs synapse refinement; its dysregulation impairs that program.

evidence.snippet: his postmemantine EEG still possessed a slow and disorganized background, but there were no asymmetries or epileptiform discharges during both wakefulness and sleep
evidence.explanation: The background slowing dissociated from the epileptiform discharges under NMDA-receptor blockade, supporting an encephalopathic origin distinct from discharge generation; the intermediates are unknown, hence the indirect link type.

edges/12.description: The diffusely slow, disorganized background indexes global cortical dysfunction from dysregulated NMDA-receptor signaling rather than discharge activity: it persisted on memantine after the epileptiform discharges had cleared.

evidence.snippet: These findings reflected progression compared to previous studies.
evidence.explanation: Serial imaging establishes that the atrophy is progressive in a patient with intractable seizures, but the intervening mechanism linking network hyperexcitability to tissue loss is not demonstrated; see the grin2a_dee_progressive_atrophy_mechanism discussion.

evidence.snippet: In our proband, this likely led to neuronal loss, motor dysfunction, cognitive impairment, and the other neurological features.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own attribution of neuronal loss to excessive excitatory drive and excitotoxicity, stated as likelihood rather than demonstration, which is why this edge keeps unknown intermediates.

edges/13.description: Sustained hyperexcitability and excessive calcium loading are the presumed but not directly demonstrated route to the progressive atrophy seen on serial MRI.

edges/14.description: Network hyperexcitability generates the frequent seizures and abundant epileptiform activity that constitute the epileptic component of the encephalopathy; the developmental component arrives through the parallel impaired-synaptic-maturation path.

evidence.snippet: Both of these cases of early-onset epileptic encephalopathy were the result of greatly increased current flow through mutant-GluN2A-containing NMDARs, leading to excessive excitatory drive, thereby inducing seizure activity and/or excitotoxicity.
evidence.explanation: States the causal chain from excessive excitatory drive to seizure activity in the two index gain-of-function cases.

edges/15.description: Hyperexcitable cortical networks discharge as the focal, characteristically drug-resistant seizures of the severe phenotype.

edges/16.description: The same hyperexcitable networks produce the tonic seizure semiology of the severe phenotype; homozygous knock-in mice die of tonic-clonic seizures.

edges/17.description: Cortical hyperexcitability drives the frequent myoclonic jerks and multifocal myoclonus; the jerks ceased when receptor overactivity was damped with memantine.

edges/18.description: Interictal spike-and-slow-wave discharges are the electrographic signature of the hyperexcitable network, and cleared on memantine while the slow background persisted.

edges/19.description: Disrupted activity-dependent synapse formation and refinement during the window in which GluN2A expression normally rises deprives every developmental domain of its instructive signal, producing delay from infancy.

edges/20.description: The failed maturation program consolidates as the moderate to profound intellectual disability of the severe phenotype; in the index case cognition did not improve even after seizure frequency fell by two thirds on memantine, consistent with a maturation deficit rather than a purely seizure-driven one.

edges/21.description: Motor circuit maturation depends on the same activity-dependent synaptic refinement; at the severe end purposeful motor development is absent.

edges/22.description: Speech and language acquisition is the most sensitive output of the disrupted maturation program across the GRIN2A spectrum; at this severe end expressive speech does not develop at all.

edges/23.description: The independently abnormal developmental trajectory is the developmental component of the developmental and epileptic encephalopathy; the seizure component arrives through the excitation-inhibition-imbalance path.

edges/24.description: The tissue-level parenchymal volume loss manifests clinically as progressive cerebral atrophy on serial MRI.

edges/25.description: Callosal thinning is part of the same progressive structural loss, accompanying the hemispheric volume reduction.

edges/26.description: The white-matter arm of the structural process: hypomyelination of the terminal zones and temporal lobes accompanies the parenchymal loss.

evidence.snippet: The diagnosis of a GRIN2A-related disorder is established in a proband by the identification of a GRIN2A heterozygous pathogenic variant on molecular genetic testing.
evidence.explanation: A heterozygous GRIN2A pathogenic variant establishes the diagnosis.

evidence.snippet: Applying the criteria of the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics to all published variants yielded 156 additional cases with pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in GRIN2A, resulting in a total of 248 individuals.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the size and curation basis of the GRIN2A variant-phenotype dataset supporting the genotype-severity model.

genes/0.notes: Heterozygous GRIN2A variants cause the disorder. At this severe end the variants are characteristically de novo missense changes in the transmembrane domains or the linkers coupling the ligand-binding domain to the channel, which predominantly confer NMDA-receptor gain-of-function. Null variants and missense variants in the amino-terminal or ligand-binding domains confer loss-of-function and predominantly produce the milder epilepsy-aphasia phenotypes. Assigning the functional class is a prerequisite for mechanism-directed treatment, because the two available precision therapies act in opposite directions.

evidence.snippet: Seizures should be treated with anti-seizure medication (ASM).
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews recommends standard anti-seizure medication for the epilepsy.

evidence.snippet: Standard anti-epileptic drug monotherapy was ineffective in the patient.
evidence.explanation: Documents the limited efficacy of standard anti-seizure monotherapy in this severe phenotype.

treatments/0.description: Seizures are treated with standard anti-seizure medications, but at this severe end of the spectrum the epilepsy is characteristically refractory: monotherapy and multi-drug regimens frequently fail to control seizures.

evidence.snippet: In vitro analysis with NMDA receptor blockers indicated that GLuN2A-L812M-containing NMDARs retained their sensitivity to the use-dependent channel blocker memantine
evidence.explanation: Establishes retained memantine sensitivity as the rationale for the therapy.

evidence.snippet: Over a 54-week period prior to memantine treatment, the proband averaged 11.1 episodes per week (SEM = 0.5). Once the full memantine dosage was achieved, there was a decrease in average seizure frequency to 3.3 per week (SEM = 0.3).
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the clinical seizure reduction with adjunct memantine.

evidence.snippet: Fourteen of 19 individuals (74%) benefited from memantine, comprising improvements in behavior (71%), development (50%), and seizure frequency (39%).
evidence.explanation: A multicentre retrospective series quantifies memantine benefit in GRIN gain-of-function variants.

evidence.snippet: Individuals with either LoF or a functionally indeterminate or no effect GRIN variant (15/34 individuals) showed significantly less benefit from memantine treatment
evidence.explanation: Restricts the indication: the benefit is confined to the gain-of-function class, so functional classification must precede treatment.

evidence.snippet: In individuals with pathogenic missense variants inhibiting the NMDAR as well as null variants, NMDA receptor blockers should be used with caution (e.g., memantine, dextromethorphan, ketamine).
evidence.explanation: Records the reciprocal caution: channel blockers are not appropriate for the loss-of-function class.

treatments/1.description: Mechanism-directed therapy for gain-of-function GRIN2A variants: the use-dependent open-channel blocker memantine reduces the excessive NMDA-receptor current. In the index patient with the linker variant p.Leu812Met, in vitro screening confirmed retained memantine sensitivity and adjunct memantine cut seizure frequency from an average of 11.1 to 3.3 episodes per week, abolished the myoclonic jerks, and cleared the frontal spike-wave discharges from the EEG. A retrospective multicentre series of 34 individuals with GRIN variants found that 74% of those with gain-of-function variants benefited, whereas those with loss-of-function or indeterminate variants benefited significantly less. Because blocker potency varies between variants (dextromethorphan and dextrorphan are more potent on p.Asn615Lys but less potent on p.Leu812Met), and because the distance of the variant from the memantine binding site tracks the response, blocker choice should be variant-specific. GeneReviews cautions that NMDA-receptor blockers be used with care in individuals with loss-of-function or null variants.

evidence.snippet: memantine inhibited GluN2A-L812M-containing NMDARs with an IC50 of 12
evidence.explanation: Direct measurement of memantine inhibition of the gain-of-function receptor, the mechanistic basis for this treatment-target edge.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Use-dependent open-channel blockade counteracts the excessive receptor activity of gain-of-function variants.

evidence.snippet: In some individuals with pathogenic loss-of-function and null GRIN2A variants, treatment with the N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) coagonist L-serine was associated with improvements in behavior, development, EEG features, and/or seizure frequency.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews names L-serine as the targeted therapy for GRIN2A loss-of-function and null variants.

evidence.snippet: Among all nine individuals with LoF missense or null variants, L-serine treatment was associated with improvements in behavior in eight (89%), in development in four (44%), and/or in EEG or seizure frequency in four (44%).
evidence.explanation: Quantifies benefit in the loss-of-function class in a GRIN2A/GRIN2B n-of-1 series.

evidence.snippet: Patients had GRIN2B, GRIN1 and GRIN2A variants (12, 6 and 5 cases, respectively).

Two caveats temper the expectation: the rescue was sex-dependent for reasons that are unexplained, and the wider question of how well induced-seizure paradigms in Grin2a mice predict human response is captured in the grin2a_dee_mouse_model_paradoxical_seizure_resistance discussion. No human efficacy result is available.

evidence.snippet: This new pathomechanistic model may ultimately help in predicting phenotype severity as well as eligibility for potential precision medicine approaches in GRIN2A-related disorders.
evidence.explanation: The authors frame the domain/function/severity relationship explicitly as a pathomechanistic model with precision-medicine consequences.

evidence.snippet: Our finding also enforced the current genotype-phenotype relationship theory

hypotheses/0.description: The prevailing pathomechanistic model for the GRIN2A spectrum holds that the protein domain in which a variant falls predicts its electrophysiological consequence, and that consequence predicts clinical severity. Missense variants in the transmembrane and linker domains (misTMD+Linker) sit in the gating machinery and the ion-permeation pathway and predominantly produce NMDA-receptor gain-of-function, yielding the severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy phenotype curated here. Missense variants in the amino-terminal or ligand-binding domains (misATD+LBD) exclusively produce loss-of-function and, together with null variants, yield the less severe epilepsy-aphasia phenotypes. This model is the basis for stratifying patients to opposite precision therapies (channel blockade versus co-agonist supplementation).

evidence.snippet: In individuals with GRIN2A-related disorders due to pathogenic missense variants activating the NMDAR (i.e., gain-of-function variants), receptor-specific agonists and other activators (e.g., L-serine) should be avoided as this could result in worsening of symptoms.
