open_questions/0.rationale:
Three observations demand an environmental co-factor and none identifies it. Incidence has fallen by roughly two thirds in the UK in sixteen years and similarly elsewhere; lesions are focal despite a germline variant in every cell; and penetrance within SQSTM1 families is incomplete. A purely genetic account explains none of these.
The candidate that has absorbed most of the effort is chronic paramyxovirus infection of the osteoclast - measles, RSV or canine distemper virus - and it has not held up. Measles RNA was reported in pagetic osteoclasts by in-situ hybridisation, but PCR failed to find paramyxovirus sequence in pagetic bone, pet ownership was not a risk factor, and a serological study of several hundred patients found no elevation of measles, distemper or RSV antibodies. The weight of evidence is against it. Weaker recent candidates - rural residence and breeding-cattle density, historical domestic coal burning - are ecological correlations without a mechanism.
This gap is unusually well posed and unusually urgent, because the exposure is disappearing on its own. Whatever it is, the population of people who encountered it is ageing out, and the natural experiment that could identify it is closing.

open_questions/1.rationale:
Zoledronic acid does what it is supposed to do: it suppresses the osteoclast, normalises ALP in most patients, and holds that for years. If the pagetic burden were caused by ongoing high turnover, that should translate into fewer fractures and better function. In PRISM-EZ it did not, and the point estimates for fracture and orthopaedic procedures moved the wrong way.
The most economical explanation is that the damage is architectural and already done. Once a site has been remodelled into expanded mosaic bone, the mechanical deficit is a property of the tissue, not of the rate at which it is turning over, and stopping the turnover does not restore the architecture. If that is right, the interesting question is not whether to suppress turnover but whether there is an earlier window - before a lesion has remodelled - in which suppression would matter. That has never been tested, because trials enrol patients with established disease and asymptomatic early disease is not systematically identified.
A second possibility, harder to exclude, is that suppressed turnover impairs repair of microdamage in already-abnormal bone, which would explain the direction of the non-significant fracture excess rather than dismissing it as noise.

open_questions/2.rationale:
This entry rests substantially on an environmental co-factor: incidence fell by two thirds in the UK in sixteen years, lesions are focal despite a germline allele in every cell, and penetrance within SQSTM1 families is incomplete. The mouse says the opposite. P394L knock-in animals develop focal, asymmetric, age-accumulating lesions with giant hypernucleated osteoclasts and no trigger of any kind, and the authors state the conclusion plainly - SQSTM1 mutations can cause a PDB-like disorder in the absence of an additional trigger.

Both observations are solid, so the interesting question is what the disagreement is made of. Three readings are open.

The first is dose. Murine penetrance is 77% in heterozygotes by 12 months; human SQSTM1 heterozygote penetrance is far lower and later. A laboratory mouse may simply sit above a threshold that most human carriers sit below, in which case the environmental factor is a modifier of penetrance rather than a necessary second hit - which would reconcile the two without either being wrong.

The second is that the environmental signal is not about susceptibility at all. Incidence here means *clinically diagnosed* incidence, and it has fallen over exactly the period in which routine biochemistry and imaging changed. Some of the decline could be ascertainment. The counter is that severity fell too - deformity 54% to 13%, fracture 36.7% to 6.7% - and ascertainment drift should make a disease look milder without changing what the severe end looks like.

The third is that the mouse models the SQSTM1-driven minority and the environmental factor operates on the sporadic majority, who have no SQSTM1 variant at all. This entry's own genetics section supports that split: SQSTM1 explains a minority of sporadic disease, and the GWAS loci together explain only about 13% of familial risk.

Nothing published distinguishes these. Recorded as a mismatch rather than resolved, because the entry's environmental claim has been softened from 'required' to 'strongly implicated' on the strength of the mouse, and that is as far as the evidence goes.

evidence.snippet: Here we show that, in PDAC, MHC-I molecules are selectively targeted for lysosomal degradation by an autophagy-dependent mechanism that involves the autophagy cargo receptor NBR1.
evidence.explanation: Primary study establishes selective antigen-presentation loss through autophagy.

steps/1.description: Selective autophagy directs MHC-I to lysosomes through NBR1, reducing surface antigen presentation and immune recognition in PDAC models. Autophagy inhibition can restore MHC-I and improve T-cell control. This can coexist with RAS-dependent and FAK-dependent regulation; pathway dominance or mutual independence has not been established.

evidence.snippet: Loss of PDAC cell-intrinsic FAK signalling promotes expression of the immunoproteasome and Major Histocompatibility Complex class-I (MHC-I), resulting in increased antigen diversity and antigen presentation by FAK-/- PDAC cells.
evidence.explanation: The primary study evaluates FAK-dependent immune regulation in pancreatic cancer models.

steps/2.description: Tumor-cell FAK signaling limits immunoproteasome expression and antigen presentation in PDAC models. FAK depletion increases antigen diversity and MHC-I presentation; combined STAT3 loss further promotes immune control. This is a complementary regulator, not evidence that RAS cannot influence MHC-I. The reported antigen-presentation effect is kinase-independent, requires nuclear FAK, and is lost in an extreme squamous phenotype; FAK kinase inhibition is therefore not equivalent to eliminating this function.

evidence.snippet: Knockout of a single cytokine, GM-CSF, specifically in basal cells recapitulated macrophage repolarization and lymphocyte recruitment observed upon basal state ablation and shrank tumors.
evidence.explanation: Basal-cell-specific genetic perturbation establishes an immune-organizing GM-CSF role in mouse PDAC. Human prognostic association does not establish the same intervention effect.

steps/3.description: Basal malignant cells can organize tumor-maintaining fibroblast, macrophage and cytokine states. Lineage tracing found greater plasticity of basal than classical cells in autochthonous mouse PDAC. Basal-state ablation, and separately basal-cell GM-CSF knockout, reprogrammed the stroma and recruited cytotoxic lymphocytes. This establishes a causal circuit in these models while leaving human state-targeting efficacy unresolved.

evidence.snippet: Blocking CD24 enhanced macrophage phagocytosis of cancer cells and significantly sensitized tumors to G12Ci treatment.
evidence.explanation: Functional antibody perturbation supports CD24-mediated adaptation in G12C/G12D-selective-inhibitor PDAC models, not a proven clinical daraxonrasib-resistance route.

steps/4.description: In KRAS-G12C-driven mouse PDAC, selective KRAS inhibition upregulated the CD24 antiphagocytic signal despite an inflamed microenvironment. CD24 blockade increased macrophage phagocytosis and sensitized tumors; related findings occurred in G12D PDAC. The preprint and final paper report the same work. This is a plausible immune-adaptation route whose relevance to clinical daraxonrasib progression remains unproven.

evidence.snippet: In contrast, KRAS G12D resistance arose through retained KRAS G12D -GTP signaling, with a decrease of cyclophilin A (CypA) protein, the binding partner required for daraxonrasib activity.
evidence.explanation: Preprint cellular evidence for cyclophilin-A protein loss in the G12D context.

steps/5.description: A preprint reports reduced cyclophilin-A protein with retained KRAS-G12D-GTP signaling in daraxonrasib-resistant PDAC cells. As cyclophilin A is required for tri-complex formation, reduced availability is a plausible drug-engagement escape mechanism. This observation does not establish that peptidyl-prolyl isomerase catalytic activity was measured or is causally required. The single clinical case in this paper instead concerns KRAS-G12R EGFR/wild-type-RAS activation.

evidence.snippet: Treatment-emergent genomic alterations in the RAS signaling pathway were observed in more than half (26 of 44; 59%) of these patients, including, most notably, mutant KRAS amplifications in one-third (16 of 44; 36%), as well as alterations in receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) (4 of 44; 9%), MAPK (11 of 44; 25%) and PI3K (4 of 44; 9%) pathways.
evidence.explanation: Frequencies apply to 44 profiled patients with prior disease control followed by progression, not all treated PDAC patients; categories overlap. Mutant-allele attribution from ctDNA is exploratory and unconfirmed, as specified in Supplementary Table 3.

evidence.snippet: Method is exploratory, and allele amplification is not confirmed.
evidence.explanation: Supplementary Table 3 qualifies mutant-versus-wild-type assignment from relative variant allele frequencies. This limitation does not negate the observed 16/44 KRAS amplification calls.

evidence.snippet: To corroborate these clinical findings, we found, or mechanistically established, concordant mechanisms of daraxonrasib resistance in human and murine preclinical models of PDAC, including mutant KRAS and MYC amplification and RTK upregulation, with these alterations guiding various combination therapy concepts.
evidence.explanation: Preclinical perturbation corroborates selected clinical candidate routes; it does not establish causality for every observed co-alteration.

steps/6.description: Increased mutant KRAS dosage can attenuate daraxonrasib suppression and restore RAS-pathway output in PDAC models. Paired ctDNA detected emergent KRAS amplification in 16/44 profiled PDAC patients after initial disease control. Assignment to the pre-existing mutant allele was inferred from variant-allele-frequency ratios; the supplementary table explicitly calls this exploratory and unconfirmed, rather than direct allele phasing in all cases. Engineered and selected PDAC models provide functional corroboration of mutant KRAS dosage. Secondary KRAS mutations were absent from the 44 PDAC cases and selected PDAC resistance models, while an engineered Ba/F3 deep mutational scan identified resistance-conferring second-site variants in a different context.

evidence.snippet: Treatment-emergent genomic alterations in the RAS signaling pathway were observed in more than half (26 of 44; 59%) of these patients, including, most notably, mutant KRAS amplifications in one-third (16 of 44; 36%), as well as alterations in receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) (4 of 44; 9%), MAPK (11 of 44; 25%) and PI3K (4 of 44; 9%) pathways.
evidence.explanation: Frequencies apply to 44 profiled patients with prior disease control followed by progression, not all treated PDAC patients; categories overlap. Mutant-allele attribution from ctDNA is exploratory and unconfirmed, as specified in Supplementary Table 3.

evidence.snippet: KRAS G12R is marked by its inability to transactivate RAS WT , and it was observed that daraxonrasib resistant KRAS G12R PDAC cells utilize EGFR/RAS WT -GTP signaling as the dominant adaptive route.
evidence.explanation: Preprint supports an allele-specific cellular route; it should not be generalized to all KRAS alleles.

evidence.snippet: a KRAS G12R PDAC patient who progressed after 10 months on daraxonrasib showed intratumoral EGFR/RAS WT activation
evidence.explanation: One-patient molecular observation, supplemented by ex-vivo toroid modeling; subsequent multiagent salvage cannot isolate trametinib benefit.

evidence.snippet: Proteomic analysis evidenced that MEK1 inhibition was accompanied by a sustained activation of the PI3K-AKT-MTOR pathway and by the activation of AXL, PDGFRa, and HER1-2 receptor tyrosine kinases (RTK) expressed in a large proportion of human PDAC samples analyzed.
evidence.explanation: Grounds the contextual analogy this node's description invokes, in PDAC rather than in another tumour type: in an inducible KRAS-G12D mouse PDAC model, MEK1 inhibition reactivates AXL, PDGFRa and HER1-2 alongside sustained PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling. The blockade is partial, MEK only, so it does not establish sufficiency of RTK reactivation against multiselective RAS(ON) inhibition.

steps/7.description: RTK signaling can contribute to daraxonrasib resistance in particular PDAC contexts. The paired 44-patient study found emergent RTK alterations in 4/44, with HER2-upregulated resistant models providing functional support. A separate preprint identified EGFR/wild-type-RAS activation in KRAS-G12R models and one patient who progressed after ten months. G12D cyclophilin-A loss is a distinct route. Earlier MEK or G12C-selective-inhibitor studies are contextual analogies and do not establish universal sufficiency against multiselective inhibition.

evidence.snippet: Analysis of relapsed tumours identified Myc copy number gain as a prevalent candidate resistance mechanism, which could be overcome by combinatorial TEAD inhibition in vitro.
evidence.explanation: Primary 2024 RMC-7977 study supplies stronger support than the systematic review cited by OpenScientist.

evidence.snippet: We also observed truncating mutations in NF1 (2 of 44; 4%), KEAP1 (2 of 44; 4%), a PTPN11 mutation or MYC amplification in one patient each (1 of 44; 2%).
evidence.explanation: MYC alteration occurs in one selected clinical case; co-occurrence and small numbers limit attribution.

steps/8.description: RMC-7977-resistant KPC tumors frequently gained Myc copies while maintaining ERK suppression. YAP-TEAD-dependent transcriptional output accompanied resistance, and TEAD cotargeting restored sensitivity in vitro. The subsequent daraxonrasib clinical study detected MYC amplification in one patient together with KRAS amplification and corroborated MYC-related resistance in models. These data support a bypass route without proving that all MYC gain is independent of RAS or that TEAD combinations benefit patients.

evidence.snippet: KRAS mutation (MT) is a major oncogenic driver in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC).
evidence.explanation: This directly supports KRAS as the central driver pathway in PDAC.

evidence.snippet: In the case of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas (PDAC), 90–92% harbor mutations in the oncogene KRAS, triggering canonical MAPK signaling.
evidence.explanation: Review-level estimate and signaling background; precise frequencies vary by assay and cohort.

evidence.snippet: PanIN development begins with Kirsten rat sarcoma viral oncogene (KRAS) mutations driving PanIN initiation. Key additional mutations in cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 2A (CDKN2A), tumor protein p53 (TP53), and mothers against decapentaplegic homolog 4 (SMAD4) disrupt cell cycle control and genomic stability, crucial for PanIN progression from low-grade to high-grade dysplasia.
evidence.explanation: This review confirms KRAS mutations as the initiating event in PanIN development, with additional tumor suppressor losses driving progression to invasive carcinoma.

steps/9.description: Activating KRAS variants favor persistent RAS-GTP signaling through RAF-MEK-ERK and additional effector networks, supporting proliferation, survival, metabolic rewiring and microenvironmental remodeling. G12D, G12V and G12R are common in PDAC, with allele-specific signaling and inhibitor responses. Most PDACs are KRAS-mutant; KRAS-wild-type cancers require separate driver characterization. KRAS signaling does not itself establish acquisition of a particular tumor-suppressor mutation or therapeutic inhibition.

evidence.snippet: Uptake of PDAC-derived exosomes by Kupffer cells caused transforming growth factor β secretion and upregulation of fibronectin production by hepatic stellate cells. This fibrotic microenvironment enhanced recruitment of bone marrow-derived macrophages.
evidence.explanation: The primary study supports exosomal MIF-driven liver niche formation and metastasis, not direct proof of lymphocyte suppression.

evidence.snippet: We found that macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF) was highly expressed in PDAC-derived exosomes, and its blockade prevented liver pre-metastatic niche formation and metastasis.
evidence.explanation: The primary study supports exosomal MIF-driven liver niche formation and metastasis, not direct proof of lymphocyte suppression.

steps/10.description: PDAC-derived exosomes carrying MIF can be taken up by Kupffer cells, inducing TGF-beta, hepatic stellate-cell fibronectin deposition and recruitment of bone-marrow-derived macrophages. This establishes a liver premetastatic niche mechanism; the cited study does not by itself establish direct exosomal suppression of dendritic cells or T cells.

evidence.snippet: While these pathways can be broadly inhibited using the pan-RAS-ON inhibitor RMC-6236, cells remained capable of developing acquired resistance where cell proliferation is uncoupled from RAS signaling.
evidence.explanation: Preprint directly models RMC-6236 resistance in cellular systems.

evidence.snippet: Finally, concurrent inhibition of KRAS with either CDK4/6 or CDK2 yields durable tumor control in vivo in xenografts derived from acquired resistant models.
evidence.explanation: Xenograft validation supports preclinical cell-cycle cotargeting, with kinase-specific responses.

steps/11.description: A preprint describes acquired RMC-6236 resistance in mixed PDAC and NSCLC models with sustained cell-cycle progression despite RAS suppression. CDK4/6 or CDK2 cotargeting restored control through distinct arrest programs; CDK2 inhibition produced more durable cytostasis in the tested settings. This is not a clinically validated combination or proof that simultaneous inhibition of all three kinases is required. CDK8-mediated microenvironmental resistance is a separate mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Through unbiased CRISPR-based screenings, we identified mTOR and JUN hyperactivation as interconnected mechanisms that overcome MAPK suppression.
evidence.explanation: CRISPR and follow-up cellular experiments support the combination-treatment scope.

evidence.snippet: Alterations in the PI3K/AKT/mTOR and JUN pathways can induce resistance to multiple combinations of MAPK pathway inhibitors
evidence.explanation: The study conclusion explicitly concerns combinations, not a proven universal monotherapy escape mechanism.

steps/12.description: CRISPR screens identify mTOR and JUN as convergent mediators of resistance to MAPK-pathway inhibitor combinations. In PDAC cells, JUN overexpression supported resistance to SHP2 plus RMC-6236; in-vivo MAP2K4 rescue used SHP2 plus ERK inhibition. The combination-specific evidence should not be recast as patient-level daraxonrasib monotherapy resistance. A separate RMC-7977 mouse study identified focal Jun gain in one resistant tumor.

evidence.snippet: Here we report mechanisms of acquired resistance to daraxonrasib monotherapy observed through targeted sequencing of over 800 genes in paired pretreatment and end of treatment circulating tumor DNA samples from 44 patients in the phase 1/2 clinical trial.
evidence.explanation: August 2026 paired clinical sequencing supersedes the July reports and earlier assessment claim that no longitudinal clinical characterization was available.

evidence.snippet: Treatment-emergent genomic alterations in the RAS signaling pathway were observed in more than half (26 of 44; 59%) of these patients, including, most notably, mutant KRAS amplifications in one-third (16 of 44; 36%), as well as alterations in receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) (4 of 44; 9%), MAPK (11 of 44; 25%) and PI3K (4 of 44; 9%) pathways.
evidence.explanation: Frequencies apply to 44 profiled patients with prior disease control followed by progression, not all treated PDAC patients; categories overlap. Mutant-allele attribution from ctDNA is exploratory and unconfirmed, as specified in Supplementary Table 3.

evidence.snippet: Notably, no acquired secondary KRAS mutations were observed, distinct from resistance profiles of mutant-selective KRAS G12C(OFF) inhibitors.
evidence.explanation: No secondary KRAS mutations were found in this selected PDAC cohort; this is not proof that such mutations are impossible.

evidence.snippet: Among the 38 patients with RAS G12, G13, or Q61 mutations, 29% (95% CI, 15 to 46) had an objective response. The median duration of response was 8.2 months (95% CI, 3.8 to 8.8), with median values of 8.1 months for progression-free survival and 15.6 months for overall survival.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the primary-nonresponse term in this node's description. Responses are finite, which is the acquired-resistance signal, but fewer than a third of treated patients had an objective response at all, so progression on daraxonrasib cannot be read as escape from an established response across the treated population.

steps/13.description: Daraxonrasib can initially control PDAC and subsequently lose efficacy through heterogeneous resistance routes. An August 2026 study profiled 44 patients with response or stable disease lasting more than three months followed by progression: 59% had treatment-emergent RAS-pathway genomic alterations, including KRAS amplification in 36%. Mutant-allele identity was inferred from variant-allele-frequency ratios by an exploratory method, not directly confirmed in all cases. These selected-cohort findings establish patient mechanisms but not universal resistance or population-wide route frequencies. Median progression-free survival alone cannot distinguish acquired resistance, primary nonresponse and death. Non-genomic, tissue-specific and low-shedding routes remain incompletely captured.

evidence.snippet: We found that dual SHP2/mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase (MEK1/2) inhibition induces major alterations in mitochondrial mass and function, impacts reactive oxygen species (ROS) homeostasis and triggers lipid peroxidase dependency.
evidence.explanation: The primary experiment concerns vertical SHP2-MEK blockade.

steps/14.description: Dual SHP2-MEK inhibition produces persistent mitochondrial changes and lipid-peroxide-defense dependency in PDAC models, with confirmation under direct RAS targeting. Sensitivity to GPX4 disruption is an exploitable treatment-induced vulnerability; it does not mean ferroptosis is already increased or that this state itself causes clinical daraxonrasib resistance. The primary intervention and model context are retained.

evidence.snippet: Mechanistically, inhibition of KRASG12D in advanced PDAC and human patient derived organoids induces FAS expression in cancer cells and facilitates CD8+ T cell-mediated death.
evidence.explanation: The final primary report directly supports FAS induction and killing, including human organoid experiments.

steps/15.description: KRAS-G12D inhibition by MRTX1133 induces FAS in malignant cells and patient-derived organoids, permitting CD8-mediated killing in PDAC models. This is drug- and model-specific evidence; the original citation to the preprint has been replaced with the final paper. CDK8-dependent FAS suppression can later oppose this response.

evidence.snippet: the tumor cells that remained exhibited increased expression of MHC class I
evidence.explanation: Flow-cytometric on-treatment finding in 6419c5 PDAC tumors after RMC-7977; this does not establish the precise molecular mediator.

steps/16.description: RMC-7977 increased MHC-I on residual malignant cells in a syngeneic PDAC model. This is direct evidence for a RAS(ON)-associated antigen-presentation change in PDAC, although the relative mediation by autophagy, FAK, interferon signaling and tumor selection remains unresolved. NSCLC daraxonrasib-elironrasib results are supplementary cross-cancer evidence, not the sole anchor.

evidence.snippet: Mechanistically, KRASG12D transcriptionally upregulated USP20 via EGR1, which simultaneously deubiquitinated and stabilised 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA reductase and ULK1, thereby orchestrating cholesterol metabolism and autophagy-associated survival.
evidence.explanation: Mechanistic preclinical experiments relate USP20 to cholesterol and autophagy; the cohort provides human-tissue context.

evidence.snippet: In preclinical PDAC models, triple therapy with GSK2643943A, MRTX1133 and anti-PD-1 elicited a robust therapeutic response and induced significant tumour regression.
evidence.explanation: Mouse combination activity remains investigational.

steps/17.description: KRAS-G12D induces EGR1-USP20, stabilizing HMG-CoA reductase and promoting cholesterol metabolism associated with CD8 exhaustion. KRAS inhibition or cholesterol blockade induces compensatory ULK1-associated autophagy; USP20 also stabilizes ULK1. This is a two-arm metabolic and survival mechanism. MRTX1133 plus USP20 inhibition and PD-1 blockade regressed tumors in preclinical models, but human tissue profiling is not evidence of clinical combination efficacy.

evidence.snippet: CDK8 imparts this resistance via induction of CXCL2 chemokine secretion, inhibition of FAS expression, and remodeling of the TME to promote immune evasion.
evidence.explanation: The mechanistic immune reversal was tested chiefly during MRTX1133 treatment.

evidence.snippet: We also provide evidence of CDK8 upregulation in PDX tumors resistant to inhibitors selective for RAS(ON) and RASG12D(ON): daraxonrasib and zoldonrasib, respectively
evidence.explanation: PDX expression supports a shared candidate node, without proving drug-specific immune mediation.

steps/18.description: Long-term MRTX1133 treatment can reverse early immune infiltration through CDK8-associated CXCL2 secretion and FAS suppression. CDK8 perturbation restores immune control in those PDAC models. Daraxonrasib-resistant PDX tumors also show CDK8 upregulation, but this does not establish the entire temporal CXCL2/FAS immune circuit under daraxonrasib or in patients.

evidence.snippet: Here, we demonstrate that Kras* targeting using MRTX1133 or Daraxonrasib recruits diverse T-cell infiltrates, including regulatory (Tregs), effector and exhausted T cells into the PDAC microenvironment.
evidence.explanation: Newer mouse PDAC evidence replaces the unsupported positive Treg-relief node.

evidence.snippet: the increase in CD4+ T cells upon RMC-7977 treatment was not attributable to this population
evidence.explanation: In this separate model the CD4 expansion did not reflect FoxP3-positive Tregs, illustrating model dependence.

steps/19.description: An August 2026 PDAC study found that MRTX1133 or daraxonrasib recruits regulatory as well as effector and exhausted T cells. In its models, CTLA-4 blockade reprogrammed effector Tregs, reduced CD8 exhaustion and supported tertiary lymphoid structures. Other checkpoint combinations were less effective. This contrasts with a different RMC-7977 model where the CD4 increase was not attributable to FoxP3-positive Tregs, so generalized Treg relief is not supported.

evidence.snippet: These observations suggest that, during adulthood, PDA stems from a combination of genetic (e.g., somatic K-Ras mutations) and nongenetic (e.g., tissue damage) events.
evidence.explanation: States the two-component model directly: the genetic lesion is modeled by the KRAS node and the nongenetic tissue-damage component is what this node is for.

evidence.snippet: There is an increased risk of PDAC in patients with CP, and incidence rates increase with CP disease duration.
evidence.explanation: The human counterpart of the mouse result, with risk rising as the inflammation persists. PARTIAL because it measures cancer incidence in inflamed pancreata rather than anything at this node itself.

steps/20.description: Inflammation and tissue injury can cooperate with oncogenic KRAS to enable acinar reprogramming and precursor formation. In one adult acinar/centroacinar KRAS-G12V mouse model, chronic pancreatitis was necessary for tumor induction. This is a model-specific requirement, not a claim that every human PDAC requires clinically recognized pancreatitis. Human chronic pancreatitis is a strong risk factor with risk estimates dependent on follow-up and case definition.

evidence.snippet: Acinar to ductal metaplasia (ADM) is the predominant form of ductal metaplasia in pancreas.
evidence.explanation: Establishes ADM as the dominant metaplastic route in this organ, which is what this node models.

evidence.snippet: suggesting that PDA originates by differentiation of acinar/centroacinar cells or their precursors into ductal-like cells
evidence.explanation: Lineage evidence that the ductal-like cells of PDAC descend from the acinar compartment, which is the transdifferentiation this node annotates.

evidence.snippet: These data demonstrate that pancreatic ductal cells, whereas exhibiting relative resistance to oncogenic Kras alone, can serve as an effective cell of origin for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma in the setting of gain-of-function mutations in p53.
evidence.explanation: Ductal-origin mouse experiments refute exclusive acinar origin.

steps/21.description: Acinar cells can lose differentiated identity and adopt ductal-like programs during injury and KRAS-driven transformation. ADM is reversible in regenerative settings and is not synonymous with cancer. Persistent oncogenic signaling can channel reprogrammed cells into PanIN. Adult ductal cells can also initiate PDAC with cooperating p53 alterations in mice; the relative contribution of these origins in humans remains unresolved.

evidence.snippet: In this study, we report that RAS(ON) multi-selective inhibition led to rapid and profound PDAC regressions in immunocompetent mice, decreasing myeloid cells and increasing T cells and macrophages in the tumor microenvironment.
evidence.explanation: Direct PDAC evidence was omitted from the immune report despite being cited in the resistance report.

evidence.snippet: MRTX1133 reverses early PDAC growth, increases intratumoral CD8+ effector T cells, decreases myeloid infiltration, and reprograms cancer-associated fibroblasts.
evidence.explanation: Final peer-reviewed MRTX1133 paper; its preprint PMID36824971 is not independent replication.

steps/22.description: MRTX1133 and RAS(ON) multiselective inhibitors can reduce suppressive myeloid subsets and increase effector lymphocytes in immunocompetent PDAC models. Total macrophage abundance can increase while state composition changes; myeloid remodeling is not equivalent to depletion of every myeloid cell. The direction and durability of individual populations vary by agent, model and time.

evidence.snippet: In this study, we report that RAS(ON) multi-selective inhibition led to rapid and profound PDAC regressions in immunocompetent mice, decreasing myeloid cells and increasing T cells and macrophages in the tumor microenvironment.
evidence.explanation: Direct PDAC evidence was omitted from the immune report despite being cited in the resistance report.

evidence.snippet: The depth and duration of tumor regression depended on T cells and conventional dendritic cells.
evidence.explanation: Depletion/genetic experiments establish immune contribution in mouse PDAC.

steps/23.description: In immunocompetent PDAC models, RAS(ON) multiselective inhibition can reduce suppressive myeloid subsets, increase tumor MHC-I and lymphocyte infiltration, and enable immune-dependent tumor control. RMC-7977 and daraxonrasib provide direct PDAC evidence. Responses and optimal checkpoint partners are model-dependent; increased Tregs and adaptive myeloid rebound can limit benefit. Patient survival from daraxonrasib monotherapy does not establish an immune-mediated clinical benefit.

evidence.snippet: This list includes the classic tumor suppressor genes CDKN2A (p16), SMAD4, and TP53, as well as genes that had not previously been implicated in pancreatic cancer development.
evidence.explanation: The landmark Jones et al. genomic analysis identified CDKN2A, SMAD4, and TP53 as core tumor suppressor genes in pancreatic cancer through global sequencing of 24 advanced pancreatic adenocarcinomas.

steps/24.description: Alterations of CDKN2A, TP53 and SMAD4 cooperate with oncogenic signaling. Loss of p16 removes restraint on CDK4/6-RB cell-cycle progression; p53 alterations weaken stress checkpoints and can confer context-dependent gain of function; SMAD4 loss changes TGF-beta responses. Reported alteration frequencies differ with cohort, assay, copy-number detection and inclusion of epigenetic silencing. These are cooperating events rather than consequences inferred from co-occurrence with KRAS.

evidence.snippet: Transcriptome and metabolomic analyses indicate that Kras(G12D) serves a vital role in controlling tumor metabolism through stimulation of glucose uptake and channeling of glucose intermediates into the hexosamine biosynthesis and pentose phosphate pathways (PPP).
evidence.explanation: Genetic KRAS withdrawal and metabolic profiling establish the growth-supporting program.

steps/25.description: KRAS supports glucose uptake and redirects intermediates toward anabolic pathways that sustain pancreatic tumor growth. This is a regulated metabolic program rather than a universal switch eliminating oxidative phosphorylation.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, we establish that the reprogramming of glutamine metabolism is mediated by oncogenic KRAS
evidence.explanation: Genetic experiments connect KRAS to the noncanonical glutamine pathway.

steps/26.description: In studied PDAC cells, glutamine-derived aspartate is routed through cytosolic GOT1, malate and pyruvate to support NADPH-dependent redox balance. Dependency varies with growth context and compensatory metabolism; this does not establish clinical efficacy of glutaminase inhibition.

evidence.snippet: The internalized protein undergoes proteolytic degradation, yielding amino acids including glutamine that can enter central carbon metabolism.
evidence.explanation: Protein uptake supplies usable metabolites in Ras-transformed cellular models.

evidence.snippet: Consistent with this hypothesis, active macropinocytosis is observed in primary human PDAC specimens.
evidence.explanation: Human tissue supports relevance, without establishing universal flux or dependency.

steps/27.description: RAS-driven macropinocytosis internalizes extracellular protein for lysosomal proteolysis and amino-acid supply. It supports growth in nutrient-poor settings and is observed in primary human PDAC specimens, complementing transport of free nutrients.

evidence.snippet: Genetic or pharmacologic inhibition of autophagy leads to increased reactive oxygen species, elevated DNA damage, and a metabolic defect leading to decreased mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence.explanation: Direct perturbation demonstrates metabolic support in the tested PDAC cells.

steps/28.description: Basal autophagy can maintain oxidative metabolism and restrain damaging reactive oxygen species in established pancreatic cancer models. Recycling also provides substrates under treatment stress. The effects of autophagy loss differ by tumor stage and genetic context; preclinical dependency is not a validated universal treatment response.

evidence.snippet: However, if these mice are challenged with a mild form of chronic pancreatitis, they develop the full spectrum of PanINs and invasive PDA.
evidence.explanation: Genetic and inflammatory cooperation supports progression in the defined mouse model.

evidence.snippet: In contrast to the lack of response to oncogenic Kras alone, simultaneous activation of Kras and mutant p53 in adult ductal epithelium generated invasive PDAC in 75% of mice as early as 2.5 months after tamoxifen administration.
evidence.explanation: Cooperating oncogenic KRAS and mutant p53 enable invasive cancer in ductal-origin mice.

steps/29.description: KRAS-mutant PanIN can progress with cooperating genetic and microenvironmental changes to invasive, gland-forming PDAC. IPMN and mucinous cystic neoplasms provide additional precursor routes. Not every precursor progresses, and a uniform obligatory mutation order or exclusive acinar origin is not established.

evidence.snippet: Here, we use organoid and mouse models to identify TGFβ and IL1 as tumor-secreted ligands that promote CAF heterogeneity.
evidence.explanation: Tumor-secreted signals establish heterogeneous stromal responses.

steps/30.description: Tumor-derived signals and local tissue interactions recruit and alter fibroblast states that deposit collagen, hyaluronan and other extracellular matrix. Dense matrix can impair perfusion, but stromal programs are heterogeneous: some support inflammation or immune exclusion and others restrain tumor growth. Fibroblast depletion and matrix digestion are not interchangeable, and neither is a generally validated treatment for PDAC.

evidence.snippet: Administering AMD3100, a CXCL12 receptor chemokine (C-X-C motif) receptor 4 inhibitor, induced rapid T-cell accumulation among cancer cells and acted synergistically with α-PD-L1 to greatly diminish cancer cells
evidence.explanation: Perturbation supports CXCL12-CXCR4-mediated immune exclusion in a mouse PDAC model.

steps/31.description: FAP-positive fibroblasts can supply CXCL12 that localizes around malignant cells and limits T-cell access. In KPC mouse tumors, CXCR4 inhibition rapidly increased T-cell accumulation and synergized with PD-L1 blockade. This identifies a specific stromal immune-exclusion circuit, not uniform behavior of all fibroblasts.

evidence.snippet: We show that IL1 induces LIF expression and downstream JAK/STAT activation to generate inflammatory CAFs and demonstrate that TGFβ antagonizes this process by downregulating IL1R1 expression and promoting differentiation into myofibroblasts.
evidence.explanation: Directly distinguishes competing CAF programs.

steps/32.description: Tumor-derived IL1 induces fibroblast LIF and JAK-STAT signaling, promoting an inflammatory CAF state. TGF-beta antagonizes this program by reducing IL1R1 and favoring myofibroblasts. Spatial exposure and plasticity generate distinct CAF niches, so fibroblast number alone is an inadequate mechanistic readout.

evidence.snippet: Together, these data demonstrate that some components of the tumor stroma can act to restrain tumor growth.
evidence.explanation: The primary genetic stromal-perturbation study establishes an important counterexample to uniformly tumor-promoting stroma.

evidence.snippet: Suppressed immune surveillance with increased CD4(+)Foxp3(+) Tregs was observed in myofibroblast-depleted mouse tumors.
evidence.explanation: Myofibroblast depletion worsened mouse disease; intervention and source scope are explicit.

steps/33.description: Some fibroblast and stromal programs constrain PDAC. Genetic SHH loss and depletion of alpha-SMA-positive myofibroblasts in distinct mouse models accelerated aggressive disease; newer interferon-response CAF work also identifies a restraining state. These findings qualify global stroma-removal strategies without proving that every myofibroblast state is protective.

evidence.snippet: We show here that this desmoplastic reaction generates inordinately high interstitial fluid pressures (IFPs), exceeding those previously measured or theorized for solid tumors, and induces vascular collapse, while presenting substantial barriers to perfusion, diffusion, and convection of small molecule therapeutics.
evidence.explanation: Primary mouse study supports a physical stromal barrier.

steps/34.description: Hyaluronan-rich stroma can elevate interstitial fluid pressure, collapse vessels and restrict delivery of nutrients and drugs in PDAC mouse models. Matrix degradation improved perfusion experimentally, but the phase III PEGPH20 trial did not improve survival, limiting direct therapeutic extrapolation.

evidence.snippet: Kras(G12D)-dependent production of GM-CSF in vivo is required for the recruitment of Gr1(+)CD11b(+) myeloid cells.
evidence.explanation: Primary mechanistic study links oncogenic KRAS to GM-CSF-dependent immune suppression.

steps/35.description: Oncogenic KRAS induces tumor-cell GM-CSF, expanding suppressive myeloid cells that constrain cytotoxic T-cell immunity in pancreatic neoplasia models. This supplies a disease-driving counterpart to the myeloid remodeling seen after KRAS inhibition.

evidence.snippet: Here, we show that PDAC-derived exosomes induce liver pre-metastatic niche formation in naive mice and consequently increase liver metastatic burden.
evidence.explanation: The primary study experimentally connects extracellular vesicles to a permissive liver niche.

steps/36.description: Invasive tumor cells disseminate and establish distant lesions, frequently in the liver and also lung or peritoneum. Colonization depends on both tumor-cell programs and organ-specific niches; metastatic-site immune composition differs from the primary tumor. A single EMT program is not obligatory for every metastatic event.

evidence.snippet: Tagged cells invaded and entered the bloodstream unexpectedly early, before frank malignancy could be detected by rigorous histologic analysis; this behavior was widely associated with epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT).
evidence.explanation: Lineage tracking establishes early dissemination in a mouse pancreatic-cancer model, not universal timing of human metastasis.

evidence.snippet: EMT suppression in the primary tumour does not alter the emergence of invasive PDAC, systemic dissemination or metastasis.
evidence.explanation: Snail/Twist deletion challenges obligatory EMT in this mouse model; it does not show that all EMT programs are irrelevant.

steps/37.description: Epithelial-mesenchymal plasticity can accompany dissemination and drug resistance, but individual EMT transcription factors have nonredundant roles. Snail or Twist deletion did not abolish metastasis in a KPC study. Early dissemination observed in mouse precursor models is not proof that all human PDAC metastasizes before invasion.

evidence.snippet: Activating the HGF/c-Met signaling pathway potentiated the expression of nerve growth factor (NGF) to recruit nerves and promote the PNI.
evidence.explanation: Direct perturbation supports tumor-nerve crosstalk.

evidence.snippet: we found that knocking down c-Met expression inhibited cancer cell migration along the nerve, reduced the damage of the sciatic nerve caused by cancer cells and protected the function of the sciatic nerve in vivo.
evidence.explanation: Mouse nerve-invasion experiments support local injury, not a clinical pain-frequency estimate.

evidence.snippet: Enhanced expression of the NGF/TrkA system may influence perineural invasion and may contribute to the pain syndrome in human pancreatic cancer.
evidence.explanation: Human tissue association supports biological relevance while preserving the authors causal uncertainty.

evidence.snippet: Preoperative pain does not predict the presence of perineural invasion or other pathologic prognostic factors in patients with resectable pancreatic adenocarcinoma.
evidence.explanation: Prospective 52-patient resectable cohort qualifies pain as a neural-invasion surrogate.

steps/38.description: Pancreatic cancer cells interact with nerves and migrate along neural structures. HGF-MET signaling can activate mTOR-NGF, promoting nerve recruitment and invasion in experimental models. PNI is associated with adverse clinical outcomes and can contribute to pain; it is not established as the universal route to distant metastasis. Human NGF/TrkA levels correlate with PNI and pain in one tissue cohort, but a prospective resectable cohort found pain did not predict PNI; clinical pain and neural invasion are not interchangeable readouts.

treatments/1.description: Combination of fluorouracil, leucovorin, irinotecan, and oxaliplatin. Used as first-line treatment for metastatic PDAC in fit patients and as adjuvant therapy after surgical resection. Provides superior survival compared to gemcitabine alone but with greater toxicity.

evidence.snippet: nab-paclitaxel plus gemcitabine significantly improved overall survival, progression-free survival, and response rate, but rates of peripheral neuropathy and myelosuppression were increased.
evidence.explanation: The Von Hoff et al. phase 3 trial demonstrated that nab-paclitaxel plus gemcitabine significantly improved overall survival (8.5 vs 6.7 months) in metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma.

treatments/2.description: Gemcitabine with nab-paclitaxel improves survival over gemcitabine alone in metastatic PDAC, with increased neuropathy and myelosuppression. Regimen selection depends on fitness and prior therapy; separate trials do not establish superior tolerability to FOLFIRINOX.

evidence.snippet: The phase III POLO study demonstrated significant progression-free survival (PFS) benefit for active olaparib maintenance therapy versus placebo for patients with metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma and a germline BRCA mutation.
evidence.explanation: The phase III POLO trial supports maintenance olaparib in germline BRCA-mutated metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma; folded in from the former Metastatic_Pancreatic_Adenocarcinoma entry.

evidence.snippet: We conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial to evaluate the efficacy of olaparib as maintenance therapy in patients who had a germline BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation and metastatic pancreatic cancer and disease that had not progressed during first-line platinum-based chemotherapy.
evidence.explanation: The POLO trial demonstrated that maintenance olaparib significantly prolonged progression-free survival in germline BRCA-mutated metastatic pancreatic cancer patients who had not progressed on platinum-based chemotherapy.

evidence.snippet: No statistically significant OS benefit was observed (median 19.0 v 19.2 months; hazard ratio [HR], 0.83; 95% CI, 0.56 to 1.22; P = .3487).
evidence.explanation: Final POLO analysis qualifies the PFS benefit with the nonsignificant OS comparison.

treatments/3.description: Maintenance olaparib improves progression-free survival in metastatic PDAC with germline BRCA1/2 pathogenic variants and no progression after at least 16 weeks of first-line platinum chemotherapy. POLO did not show a statistically significant overall-survival benefit in the final analysis. This evidence does not extend automatically to every DNA-repair alteration.

evidence.snippet: The purpose of this study is to evaluate the safety and efficacy of a novel RAS(ON) inhibitor compared to standard(s) of care (SOC) treatment.
evidence.explanation: ClinicalTrials.gov documents RASolute 302 as a phase 3 evaluation of the RAS(ON) inhibitor daraxonrasib versus standard-of-care chemotherapy in previously treated metastatic PDAC.

evidence.snippet: Daraxonrasib is an oral RAS(ON) multiselective, tri-complex inhibitor of the active guanosine triphosphate-bound state of mutant and wild-type RAS.
evidence.explanation: Establishes daraxonrasib's mechanism of action as a RAS(ON) multiselective tri-complex inhibitor of the active GTP-bound state of mutant and wild-type RAS, the basis for its target_mechanisms link to KRAS-centered signaling.

evidence.snippet: The median overall survival in the RAS G12 population was 13.2 months with daraxonrasib and 6.6 months with chemotherapy, and the median overall survival in the overall population was 13.2 months and 6.7 months, respectively; the hazard ratio was 0.40 in both populations (P<0.001).
evidence.explanation: RASolute 302 demonstrated a significant overall survival benefit for daraxonrasib over chemotherapy (hazard ratio for death 0.40) in previously treated metastatic PDAC.

treatments/4.description: Daraxonrasib is a cyclophilin-A-dependent inhibitor of active GTP-bound mutant and wild-type RAS. In phase III RASolute 302 for previously treated metastatic PDAC, median overall survival was 13.2 versus 6.6 months in the RAS G12 population (hazard ratio 0.40); median progression-free survival was 7.3 versus 3.5 months. These clinical outcomes establish treatment efficacy, not a universal resistance mechanism or an immune basis for survival benefit.

evidence.snippet: Daraxonrasib is an oral RAS(ON) multiselective, tri-complex inhibitor of the active guanosine triphosphate-bound state of mutant and wild-type RAS.
evidence.explanation: The RASolute 302 report describes daraxonrasib's mechanism as direct inhibition of the active GTP-bound RAS state driven by mutant KRAS in PDAC.

treatments/4/targets/0.description: Daraxonrasib directly inhibits the active RAS(ON) state produced by oncogenic KRAS codon-12 mutations, the initiating driver of PDAC, suppressing constitutive RAS-MAPK signaling.

evidence.snippet: In this study, we report that RAS(ON) multi-selective inhibition led to rapid and profound PDAC regressions in immunocompetent mice, decreasing myeloid cells and increasing T cells and macrophages in the tumor microenvironment.
evidence.explanation: Direct PDAC evidence was omitted from the immune report despite being cited in the resistance report.

treatments/4/targets/1.description: Preclinical PDAC immune remodeling follows RAS inhibition; this is not an inferred immune mechanism for the phase III survival effect.

evidence.snippet: Here, we demonstrate that Kras* targeting using MRTX1133 or Daraxonrasib recruits diverse T-cell infiltrates, including regulatory (Tregs), effector and exhausted T cells into the PDAC microenvironment.
evidence.explanation: Newer mouse PDAC evidence replaces the unsupported positive Treg-relief node.

treatments/4/targets/2.description: Treg recruitment is a model-dependent adaptation documented with daraxonrasib and MRTX1133.

evidence.snippet: Cancer vaccine ELI-002 2P enhances lymph node delivery and immune response using amphiphile (Amph) modification of G12D and G12R mutant KRAS (mKRAS) peptides (Amph-Peptides-2P) together with CpG oligonucleotide adjuvant (Amph-CpG-7909).
evidence.explanation: Describes the mutant-KRAS amphiphile vaccine platform evaluated in the phase 1 AMPLIFY-201 trial.

treatments/5.description: The phase I AMPLIFY-201 trial evaluated ELI-002 2P, an amphiphile G12D/G12R KRAS peptide vaccine plus CpG adjuvant, in patients with molecular residual KRAS-mutated pancreatic or colorectal cancer. It induced KRAS-specific T-cell responses. This early mixed-cancer study does not establish prevention in healthy high-risk individuals or randomized recurrence/survival benefit.

evidence.snippet: Kras* inhibition induces T-cell influx and offers a therapeutic window to specifically prime PDAC to anti-CTLA4 immune checkpoint blockade efficacy, in contrast to anti-PD1, anti-Tim3, anti-Lag3, anti-Vista, and anti-4-1BB agonist combination therapy.
evidence.explanation: The newer model-specific comparison qualifies general checkpoint synergy.

treatments/6.description: Checkpoint combinations with RAS inhibitors are supported by mouse PDAC experiments. RMC-7977/daraxonrasib plus PD-1-based therapy worked in one study, whereas a later study found CTLA-4 blockade specifically effective and associated with Treg reprogramming and tertiary lymphoid structures. Regimen, model, timing and checkpoint partner matter. These results do not establish routine clinical daraxonrasib-checkpoint treatment.

evidence.snippet: the combination of RAS(ON) multi-selective inhibitors with immunotherapy conferred deeper and more durable tumor regressions, including complete responses not seen with either treatment alone.
evidence.explanation: Direct immunocompetent PDAC combination evidence.

treatments/6/targets/0.description: Experimental combinations deepen immune-dependent tumor control.

evidence.snippet: Median overall survival was 11·1 months (95% CI 10·0-12·1) with NALIRIFOX versus 9·2 months (8·3-10·6) with nab-paclitaxel-gemcitabine
evidence.explanation: Randomized phase III evidence supports this contemporary chemotherapy option.

treatments/7.description: Liposomal irinotecan, oxaliplatin, fluorouracil and leucovorin is a first-line option for fit patients with metastatic PDAC. NAPOLI 3 improved median overall survival to 11.1 versus 9.2 months compared with gemcitabine-nab-paclitaxel; high-grade toxicity was frequent in both groups.

evidence.snippet: 15 of 36 patients (42%; 95% CI, 25 to 59) with pancreatic cancer
evidence.explanation: Pancreatic-cancer subgroup response in the NRG1-fusion-selected eNRGy trial.

treatments/8.description: The HER2/HER3 bispecific antibody targets the NRG1-fusion signaling subset. In the phase II eNRGy trial, 15 of 36 evaluable pancreatic-cancer patients responded (42%); this single-arm molecularly selected result does not describe unselected PDAC.

evidence.snippet: The overall response rate by Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors was 77% (7/9).
evidence.explanation: A retrospective nine-patient MSI-high advanced pancreatic-cancer series supports subset activity; the small selected denominator limits precision.

evidence.snippet: Eight out of nine patients received single-agent pembrolizumab (8/9), while one received ipilimumab plus nivolumab.
evidence.explanation: The agent binding identifies the predominant treatment in this small retrospective series; the nine-patient outcome includes one different checkpoint regimen.

treatments/9.description: Mismatch-repair deficiency or high microsatellite instability identifies a small immune-treatment-sensitive subset. Responses in selected case series should not be generalized to microsatellite-stable PDAC or used as a population-wide response estimate. Pembrolizumab was used in eight of the nine immunotherapy-treated patients in the cited series; one received ipilimumab plus nivolumab, so the pooled response rate is not a pembrolizumab-only estimate.

evidence.snippet: Improving the nutritional status, either with parenteral nutrition or oral supplementation, can increase the body weight, skeletal muscle mass, fat mass and quality of life, facilitating the administration of chemotherapy without interruption.
evidence.explanation: The review background supports nutritional supplementation as supportive care. This entry concerns dietary counseling and oral support; parenteral nutrition is a separate medical route and is not represented by the BEHAVIORAL modality.

treatments/10.description: Assess weight loss and dietary intake and provide individualized nutritional counseling and oral supplementation. Nutritional support complements treatment of exocrine insufficiency; it is not itself pancreatic enzyme replacement.

evidence.snippet: The pooled prevalence of pancreatic exocrine insufficiency in advanced pancreatic cancer was 72% (95% confidence interval: 55-86%)
evidence.explanation: Meta-analysis supports substantial exocrine insufficiency specifically in advanced pancreatic cancer; heterogeneity and tumor location limit generalization to all PDAC.

evidence.snippet: Patients with unresectable PC receiving chemotherapy were randomly assigned to pancrelipase and nonpancrelipase groups.
evidence.explanation: The randomized trial establishes the specific enzyme preparation used in this pancreatic-cancer population.

evidence.snippet: In this randomized controlled trial, pancrelipase failed to improve the change in BMI at 8 weeks in PC patients receiving chemotherapy.
evidence.explanation: The null primary endpoint prevents presenting enzyme replacement as a proven general weight-gain or survival treatment; clinical use for exocrine insufficiency is a separate indication.

treatments/11.description: Pancreatic enzyme replacement, including pancrelipase, is used for exocrine insufficiency and maldigestion when indicated. Mixed observational/trial pooled survival associations do not establish a causal survival benefit; an 88-patient randomized trial of pancrelipase in unresectable pancreatic cancer did not improve the primary eight-week BMI endpoint.

evidence.snippet: Pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT) is the standard treatment for PEI.
evidence.explanation: The review describes symptomatic enzyme replacement for exocrine insufficiency, independently of uncertain survival benefit.

treatments/11/targets/0.description: Oral enzyme replacement supplies digestive enzymes to compensate for inadequate endogenous pancreatic enzyme delivery; it does not restore destroyed pancreatic tissue.

evidence.snippet: In the event of biliary obstruction, endoscopic placement of a fully covered, self-expandable metallic biliary stent is suggested
evidence.explanation: Guideline addresses biliary obstruction.

treatments/12.description: Endoscopic placement of a fully covered self-expandable metallic biliary stent can relieve malignant biliary obstruction. Select procedural drainage according to anatomy, symptoms and the clinical treatment plan.

evidence.snippet: In the event of biliary obstruction, endoscopic placement of a fully covered, self-expandable metallic biliary stent is suggested
evidence.explanation: Guideline addresses biliary obstruction.

treatments/12/targets/0.description: Biliary stenting bypasses the obstructed segment and restores drainage in patients with malignant biliary obstruction.

evidence.snippet: Effective pain control is strongly recommended and should involve a pain control specialist when required
evidence.explanation: Guideline supports active specialist pain management.

treatments/13.description: Provide individualized pain assessment and specialist-guided multimodal analgesia alongside cancer-directed therapy. This supportive-care category spans medication and procedural approaches, so it does not designate one pharmacologic platform or a single therapeutic agent.

evidence.snippet: a combination of selective inhibitors of KRAS (RMC-6236/daraxonrasib), EGFR family (afatinib), and STAT3 (SD36) induced the complete regression of orthotopic PDAC tumors with no evidence of tumor resistance for over 200 d posttreatment.
evidence.explanation: Corrected republication supports pharmacologic mouse-model durability; no human efficacy or permanent cure is established.

treatments/14.description: Daraxonrasib, afatinib and the STAT3 degrader SD36 produced prolonged regressions in orthotopic, genetically engineered and patient-derived xenograft PDAC models. This corrected primary study also tested genetic RAF1/EGFR/STAT3 ablation. It supports combination research, not routine patient treatment or proof that immunity is irrelevant.

evidence.snippet: a combination of selective inhibitors of KRAS (RMC-6236/daraxonrasib), EGFR family (afatinib), and STAT3 (SD36) induced the complete regression of orthotopic PDAC tumors with no evidence of tumor resistance for over 200 d posttreatment.
evidence.explanation: The corrected mouse-model study identifies daraxonrasib as the KRAS/RAS-directed component of the combination. This pharmacologic target link does not establish acquired amplification as a consequence of the initiating mutation or identify a human resistance frequency.

treatments/14/targets/0.description: Daraxonrasib inhibits active RAS within the experimental daraxonrasib-afatinib-SD36 combination. Linking the same treatment to RAS signaling and observed resistance prevention connects the experimental resistance branch without asserting that initiating KRAS activation causes acquired amplification in untreated tumors.
