evidence.snippet: despite the absence of functional RPE65 isomerohydrolase and the subsequent inability of the retinal pigment epithelium cells to provide sufficient 11-cis retinal to the photoreceptors, the photoreceptors degenerate slowly, so that phenotypic recovery is possible through restoration of the missing enzyme to the retinal pigment epithelium cells.
evidence.explanation: This clinical study establishes that photoreceptors degenerate slowly in the absence of RPE65 activity; the slow degeneration rate explains why gene therapy can rescue function even in older patients with residual viable retina.

edges/4.description: Chronic 11-cis-retinal depletion produces ongoing rod and cone metabolic stress and drives progressive photoreceptor loss, starting with rod-dominant degeneration that eventually extends to cone loss and outer retinal atrophy.

evidence.snippet: with 50% of individuals being legally blind (visual acuity of 20/200 and/or visual fields extending <20 degrees from fixation) by age 20 years.
evidence.explanation: The GeneReview's natural-history criterion for legal blindness is stated in terms of visual fields constricted to under 20 degrees from fixation by age 20, documenting progressive field loss as an outcome of the ongoing photoreceptor degeneration rather than a static finding.

edges/5.description: Rod photoreceptors are densest outside the macula, so rod-dominant degeneration removes peripheral retinal sensitivity first and the visual field constricts progressively toward fixation.

evidence.snippet: patients may become photophobic, especially in response to diffuse light, such as occurs with cloudy weather
evidence.explanation: This pathophysiology review places photophobia in the mid-stage of rod-cone degeneration, supporting it as a downstream consequence of progressive photoreceptor loss rather than a presenting feature.

edges/6.description: Photophobia appears as cone degeneration advances in the mid-stage of the rod-cone dystrophy, rather than at presentation. It is a variable feature and is recorded here as a mid-stage consequence of degeneration, not as an early diagnostic sign.

evidence.snippet: all affected individuals are legally blind by the fourth decade and many have complete loss of vision (i.e., no light perception).
evidence.explanation: The GeneReview confirms that the natural history of RPE65-related LCA inevitably progresses to legal blindness and profound visual loss by adulthood.

edges/7.description: Progressive rod then cone loss produces night blindness, peripheral field constriction, and ultimately loss of central vision; most LCA2 individuals are legally blind by the fourth decade.

evidence.snippet: Affected infants often have high hyperopia, or less commonly high myopia, suggesting impaired emmetropisation.
evidence.explanation: The review reports the observation (high hyperopia in affected infants) and offers impaired emmetropisation as the explanation, phrased as a suggestion rather than a demonstrated mechanism. The causal edge is recorded at that strength and graded INDIRECT accordingly.

edges/8.description: Emmetropisation - the visually driven reduction of refractive error over infancy and early childhood - depends on retinal image quality, so an eye that receives almost no usable visual input in the first years fails to emmetropise and remains highly hyperopic.

evidence.snippet: Most children with RPE65 deficiency have an EOSRD phenotype with profound night blindness from birth but residual cone-mediated vision and often mild if any nystagmus.
evidence.explanation: The review reports the association in the informative direction: where biallelic RPE65 deficiency leaves residual cone-mediated vision, nystagmus is mild or absent. The claim that early visual deprivation causes the nystagmus follows from that covariation rather than being asserted directly, so this is graded INDIRECT.

edges/9.description: Nystagmus in LCA2 is a consequence of profound visual deprivation during the critical period for fixation development, not an independent oculomotor lesion. Its severity tracks the amount of residual central vision, so it is prominent in infantile-onset LCA2 and mild or absent where cone-mediated vision is preserved.

evidence.snippet: The RPE65 gene encodes all-trans retinyl ester isomerase, an enzyme crucial to the retinoid cycle.
evidence.explanation: This paper directly identifies RPE65 as the causative gene encoding a critical retinoid cycle enzyme, confirming the gene-disease relationship.

evidence.snippet: The diagnosis of autosomal recessive RPE65-related retinal degeneration is established in a proband with suggestive findings and biallelic pathogenic variants in RPE65 identified by molecular genetic testing.
evidence.explanation: The GeneReview confirms RPE65 as the causative gene for the autosomal recessive form and establishes molecular genetic testing as the diagnostic standard.

evidence.snippet: Voretigene neparvovec gene replacement improved functional vision in RPE65-mediated inherited retinal dystrophy previously medically untreatable.
evidence.explanation: The phase 3 randomised controlled trial demonstrated that voretigene neparvovec significantly improved functional vision (multi-luminance mobility testing) and full-field light sensitivity in patients with RPE65-mediated retinal dystrophy, forming the basis of FDA approval.

evidence.snippet: 13 (65%) of 20 intervention participants, but no control participants, passed MLMT at the lowest luminance level tested (1 lux), demonstrating maximum possible improvement
evidence.explanation: The primary efficacy endpoint showed that 65% of voretigene-treated participants achieved maximum possible improvement on the multi-luminance mobility test (passing at 1 lux), while no control participants did, demonstrating the clinical magnitude of gene therapy benefit.

evidence.snippet: Subretinal gene supplementation therapy for individuals between ages 12 months and 65 years with retinal degeneration known to be associated with biallelic RPE65 pathogenic variants.
evidence.explanation: The GeneReview confirms the approved gene therapy indication and age range, consistent with the subretinal delivery approach established in the phase 3 trial.

evidence.snippet: sustained results for up to 7.5 years for the full-field light sensitivity threshold test and 5 years for the multi-luminance mobility test in the Phase I and Phase III trials, respectively
evidence.explanation: This systematic review of voretigene neparvovec long-term outcomes documents sustained functional improvements for up to 7.5 years (FST) and 5 years (MLMT) across Phase I and Phase III clinical trials, confirming durable efficacy.

evidence.snippet: Thirty-five patients (34%) experienced ocular treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs), most frequently related to chorioretinal atrophy
evidence.explanation: The prospective PERCEIVE real-world registry (n=103 patients) documents the real-world safety profile of voretigene neparvovec; chorioretinal atrophy is the most frequent ocular adverse event, occurring in 12.6% of patients, which is important for post-treatment monitoring.

evidence.snippet: Improvements in both navigational abilities and light sensitivity were evident within the first 30 days after subretinal delivery and remained stable for 1 year, as they have for at least 3 years in the participants of the phase 1 follow-on trial.
evidence.explanation: This states the limit of what the randomised comparison established. The controlled endpoint was change at 1 year; stability beyond that point is carried by the uncontrolled phase 1 follow-on cohort, not by the randomised trial. Durability claims longer than a year in this entry therefore rest on extension and registry data rather than on the pivotal trial.

evidence.snippet: Other RPE65 gene therapy trials, which were administered to only one eye per individual using different gene constructs, vector formulations, or surgical approaches, have shown improvements in retinal function but variable durability of effect.
evidence.explanation: The trial report's own introduction records that earlier RPE65 gene therapy trials, using different constructs and surgical approaches, showed improved retinal function but variable durability of effect. This is the caveat the pivotal trial was not designed to resolve, and it is quoted from that paper's background rather than from its results.

evidence.snippet: most studies at later intervals have shown a lack of durability of the improvements, with continuing retinal degeneration even in patients with improved retinal function.
evidence.explanation: Recorded as a REFUTE against any reading of this treatment as arresting the degeneration. Reviewing the four phase 1 RPE65 gene therapy trials, this paper reports that most later follow-up showed a lack of durability of the functional improvements, with retinal degeneration continuing even in eyes whose retinal function had improved. Gene supplementation restores chromophore regeneration; on this evidence it does not demonstrably stop the photoreceptor loss, which is why treating while photoreceptors remain is the operative clinical point. Graded INDIRECT because the cohorts quoted are the phase 1 trials rather than the approved product's own programme.

evidence.snippet: paediatric patients retain more viable cells, present a less severe disease stage and show the highest potential for improvements, making them the most suitable candidates for treatment
evidence.explanation: This scoping review of real-world eligibility for voretigene neparvovec identifies pediatric patients as optimal candidates due to greater photoreceptor viability, supporting early evaluation and intervention in children with confirmed biallelic RPE65 mutations.

evidence.snippet: Pooled evidence demonstrated statistically significant improvements in full-field stimulus threshold testing of 2.2 log10cd.s.m-2 (95% CI -2.87 to -1.53; P < 0.001) and in visual acuity of 0.08 logMAR (95% CI -0.16-0; P = 0.040) in patients post treatment. Chorioretinal atrophy, a complication not observed in clinical trials, was reported in a subset of studies and occurred in 0.30 (95% CI 0.10-0.51; P < 0.001) for chorioretinal atrophy located anywhere
evidence.explanation: A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of post-approval voretigene neparvovec outcomes. The quoted sentences carry both halves of the claim: pooled improvement in full-field stimulus threshold and in visual acuity, and a pooled chorioretinal atrophy proportion of 0.30 for atrophy anywhere in the retina - a complication the pivotal trials did not report. The chorioretinal atrophy signal is independently carried by the PERCEIVE registry item above.

treatments/0.description: Subretinal AAV2-mediated gene supplementation therapy delivering a codon-optimized human RPE65 cDNA under control of a hybrid promoter, administered bilaterally by subretinal injection. Indicated for biallelic RPE65 mutation-associated retinal dystrophy in patients aged 12 months or older with sufficient viable retina. FDA approved December 2017 (Luxturna, Spark Therapeutics) — the first FDA-approved gene therapy for an inherited disease. Perioperative oral prednisone is used to attenuate immune responses.

evidence.snippet: Healthy balanced diet to reach the minimum reference daily intake (RDI) for nutrients. Docosahexaenoic acid / eicosapentaenoic acid supplements up to 500 mg/day as well as lutein supplements up to 10 mg/day can be considered if dietary intake is not sufficient.
evidence.explanation: The GeneReview describes supportive management including dietary supplements as standard of care alongside or in lieu of gene therapy, alongside early referral to low vision services.

treatments/1.description: Low vision aids, orientation and mobility training, and educational supports for the visually impaired are core components of management for patients not eligible for or not yet treated with gene therapy. Dietary interventions including docosahexaenoic acid and lutein supplements have been considered supportively, and children should be monitored with routine ophthalmological follow-up.

evidence.snippet: Evaluation of relatives at risk: It is appropriate to clarify the genetic status of apparently unaffected older and younger at-risk sibs in order to identify those who have biallelic RPE65 pathogenic variants and may benefit from early evaluation, counseling, and timely consideration of subretinal gene supplementation therapy.
evidence.explanation: The GeneReview explicitly recommends genetic status clarification in at-risk siblings to enable early evaluation and gene therapy consideration, establishing genetic counseling as a core management component.

treatments/2.description: Genetic counseling is indicated for affected individuals and their families to clarify the inheritance pattern (autosomal recessive), reproductive risk (25% recurrence for parents of an affected child), and to identify at-risk siblings who may benefit from early evaluation and timely gene therapy consideration.

evidence.snippet: VEXAS syndrome is attributed to somatic mutations in methionine-41 of UBA1, the major E1 enzyme that initiates ubiquitylation.
evidence.explanation: Localizes the driving somatic variants to methionine-41 of UBA1, the E1 ubiquitin-activating enzyme.

evidence.snippet: syndrome, due to mutations in UBA1 gene, identified the cause of 8 % of the patients with a clinical diagnosis of RP
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the VEXAS/UBA1 contribution at ~8% of clinically diagnosed RP, supporting that RP is more than one disease.

steps/0.description: A distinct, parallel mechanism operates in a subset (~8%) of patients given a clinical diagnosis of relapsing polychondritis. Somatic mutations at methionine-41 of UBA1 in myeloid-lineage cells dysregulate ubiquitylation and drive a myeloid/innate-immune-predominant systemic autoinflammation (VEXAS syndrome) that produces chondritis clinically indistinguishable from classic RP. Unlike the HLA-driven adaptive pathway, this arm is hematopoietic and autoinflammatory rather than autoimmune, and feeds into the same innate effector phase.

evidence.snippet: causing the degradation of proteins and the release of cryptic cartilage antigens
evidence.explanation: Describes how environmental triggers expose cryptic cartilage antigens that initiate autoimmunity in predisposed individuals.

steps/1.description: In a genetically predisposed host (HLA-DR4), mechanical, chemical, or infectious insults to cartilage cause degradation of matrix proteins and the release of normally sequestered ("cryptic") cartilage antigens, providing the initiating antigenic stimulus that breaks immune tolerance. This is the upstream event of the cartilage-directed autoimmune cascade.

evidence.snippet: Autoantibodies anti-type II, IX and XI collagens, anti-matrilin-1 and anti-COMPs (cartilage oligomeric matrix proteins) have been highlighted in increased titers, being correlated with disease activity and considered prognostic factors.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the cartilage-matrix autoantigens (type II/IX/XI collagen, matrilin-1, COMP) targeted by autoantibodies that correlate with activity.

evidence.snippet: relapsing polychondritis being considered a TH1-mediated condition
evidence.explanation: Establishes the Th1-skewed adaptive immune polarization underlying the cartilage-directed response.

evidence.snippet: Relapsing polychondritis is a rare, immune-mediated, multisystemic disease characterized by recurrent inflammation of cartilaginous and proteoglycan-rich tissues.
evidence.explanation: Establishes relapsing polychondritis as an immune-mediated, multisystemic disease targeting cartilaginous and proteoglycan-rich tissues.

steps/2.description: Loss of tolerance to cartilage matrix produces both humoral and cellular autoimmunity. Autoantibodies against type II/IX/XI collagen, matrilin-1, and cartilage oligomeric matrix protein (COMP) arise in titers that track disease activity, while CD4+ T cells drive a Th1-polarized response (IFN-γ, IL-12, IL-2). This adaptive arm orchestrates the downstream effector inflammation.

evidence.snippet: Innate immunity cells, neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages, natural killer lymphocytes and eosinophils have been found in the perichondrium and cartilage, together with activated antigen-presenting cells, C3 deposits and immunoglobulins.
evidence.explanation: Documents innate immune infiltration of perichondrium/cartilage with complement (C3) and immunoglobulin deposition.

steps/3.description: The adaptive response recruits innate effectors — neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages, and natural killer cells — into the perichondrium and cartilage, accompanied by complement (C3) and immunoglobulin deposition. This effector phase delivers the tissue-damaging machinery to both cartilaginous and vascular targets.

evidence.snippet: Relapsing polychondritis is a rare, systemic autoimmune condition characterized by recurrent inflammation of cartilaginous tissues.
evidence.explanation: Recurrent destructive inflammation of cartilaginous tissues is the defining outcome of the effector phase.

evidence.snippet: Relapsing polychondritis is a rare immunologic disorder that can involve all cartilage and proteoglycan-rich tissues.
evidence.explanation: Supports the broad cartilage/proteoglycan-rich tissue distribution of matrix destruction.

steps/4.description: Matrix-degrading enzymes (e.g., MMPs, cathepsins) and chondrocyte apoptosis progressively destroy cartilage extracellular matrix at the ear, nose, larynx, tracheobronchial tree, and joints. Recurrent destructive flares yield the chondritis and structural deformities (saddle nose, airway malacia, ear deformity) that define the disease.

evidence.snippet: Relapsing polychondritis may also affect cardiac valves and large vessels with the aorta being most frequently involved.
evidence.explanation: Establishes cardiac valve and large-vessel (predominantly aortic) involvement as part of the disease's systemic reach.

evidence.snippet: it can also impact organs that aren't primarily cartilage-based, such as blood vessels, skin, inner ear, and eyes
evidence.explanation: Confirms extension of inflammation beyond cartilage to blood vessels and other proteoglycan-rich/non-cartilage organs.

steps/5.description: The effector inflammation also targets proteoglycan-rich cardiovascular structures. Inflammation of the aortic wall (aortitis) and cardiac valves produces medial degeneration, progressive aortic dilation and aneurysm, and valvular regurgitation. Large-vessel/aortic disease is the most serious systemic complication and a leading cause of disease-related death through aortic dissection or rupture.

edges/0.description: Exposed cryptic cartilage antigens are presented to T cells and break tolerance, driving the adaptive autoimmune response.

edges/1.description: Adaptive autoimmunity recruits innate effector cells and activates complement at cartilage and proteoglycan-rich sites.

edges/2.description: Innate effectors and proteases degrade cartilage matrix and kill chondrocytes at cartilaginous sites.

edges/3.description: The same effector inflammation attacks proteoglycan-rich aortic wall and cardiac valve tissue, producing the cardiovascular disease arm.

edges/4.description: Mutant-UBA1 myeloid cells amplify innate effector inflammation that converges on the same cartilage-damaging effector phase.

evidence.snippet: HLA-DR4 being considered an allele that confers a major risk of disease occurrence
evidence.explanation: Identifies HLA-DR4 as the major genetic risk allele for relapsing polychondritis.

genes/0.notes: Idiopathic relapsing polychondritis is not Mendelian; susceptibility is polygenic with a major contribution from the MHC class II region. HLA-DR4 (an HLA-DRB1 allele group) is the most strongly associated risk allele, consistent with an antigen-presentation–driven, Th1-polarized autoimmune response against cartilage matrix proteins.

evidence.snippet: Recently, it has been associated with an autoinflammatory disease known as vacuoles, E1 enzyme, X-linked, autoinflammatory, somatic syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Documents the recently recognized association between relapsing polychondritis and VEXAS syndrome.

evidence.snippet: requiring detection of somatic ubiquitin-like modifier-activating enzyme 1 gene mutations
evidence.explanation: Identifies somatic UBA1 (ubiquitin-like modifier-activating enzyme 1) mutations as the molecular basis of the VEXAS overlap.

evidence.snippet: syndrome, due to mutations in UBA1 gene, identified the cause of 8 % of the patients with a clinical diagnosis of RP
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the VEXAS/UBA1 contribution at ~8% of patients clinically diagnosed with relapsing polychondritis.

evidence.snippet: VEXAS syndrome is attributed to somatic mutations in methionine-41 of UBA1, the major E1 enzyme that initiates ubiquitylation.
evidence.explanation: Localizes the recurrent somatic variants to methionine-41 of UBA1, the E1 ubiquitin-activating enzyme.

evidence.snippet: Sanger sequencing detected the somatic UBA1 variant c.122T > C (p.Met41Thr) in two male patients
evidence.explanation: Documents the specific recurrent somatic variant c.122T>C (p.Met41Thr) in RP patients with VEXAS.

genes/1.notes: A subset of patients, characteristically older men with concurrent myelodysplastic syndrome, harbor somatic mutations in UBA1 (the ubiquitin-like modifier-activating enzyme 1 gene) that define VEXAS syndrome (vacuoles, E1 enzyme, X-linked, autoinflammatory, somatic). VEXAS frequently presents with chondritis indistinguishable from relapsing polychondritis, so somatic UBA1 testing is now recommended in this clinical context. UBA1 is not a cause of classic idiopathic relapsing polychondritis.

evidence.snippet: managed effectively with a short course of oral or topical corticosteroids
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates corticosteroid responsiveness of chondritis flares.

evidence.snippet: Corticosteroid therapy elicited prompt clinical and biochemical response.
evidence.explanation: Confirms rapid clinical and biochemical response to corticosteroids in active disease.

treatments/0.description: Systemic corticosteroids are the mainstay for controlling acute chondritis flares; milder localized episodes may respond to short courses of oral or topical corticosteroids, while severe organ-threatening disease requires higher-dose systemic therapy and steroid-sparing immunosuppression.

evidence.snippet: While MTX had slightly less efficacy, it is one of the drugs for which data are the most robust.
evidence.explanation: Systematic review identifies methotrexate as the treatment with the most robust supporting evidence (pooled response rate ~56%).

evidence.snippet: no randomised clinical trial has been conducted to date and treatment remains empirical
evidence.explanation: Establishes that relapsing polychondritis treatment is empirical, lacking randomized trial evidence.

treatments/1.description: Methotrexate is a conventional immunosuppressant used as a steroid-sparing agent. Because no randomized trial exists for relapsing polychondritis, treatment is empirical; methotrexate is among the agents with the most robust supporting data, with a pooled response rate of ~56% across observational studies.

evidence.snippet: ABT, TCZ and TNFi were the drugs associated with the best outcomes.
evidence.explanation: Systematic review identifies TNF inhibitors among the biologics with the best outcomes (pooled response rate ~64%).

evidence.snippet: A significantly higher survival rate was seen in patients administered biologics than without
evidence.explanation: In airway-involved RP, biologic therapy was associated with significantly improved survival.

evidence.snippet: The early administration of biologics shows promise in preventing severe airway disorders that require airway stenting.
evidence.explanation: Supports early biologic therapy to prevent severe airway disease and avoid stenting.

treatments/2.description: Tumor necrosis factor inhibitors (TNFi) are among the biologic agents associated with the best outcomes in relapsing polychondritis, with a pooled response rate of ~64%.

evidence.snippet: ABT, TCZ and TNFi were the drugs associated with the best outcomes.
evidence.explanation: Tocilizumab (TCZ) is identified among the biologics with the best outcomes (pooled response rate ~66%).

treatments/3.description: Tocilizumab, an anti-interleukin-6 receptor monoclonal antibody, is among the biologics associated with the best outcomes in relapsing polychondritis (pooled response rate ~66%).

evidence.snippet: ABT, TCZ and TNFi were the drugs associated with the best outcomes.
evidence.explanation: Abatacept (ABT) is identified among the biologics with the best outcomes (pooled response rate ~72%).

evidence.snippet: ABT efficacy must be interpreted in light of the small number of patients treated.
evidence.explanation: Notes the small sample size limiting confidence in the abatacept estimate.

treatments/4.description: Abatacept (a CTLA4-Ig T-cell costimulation modulator) showed the highest pooled response rate (~72%) in the systematic review, though this estimate rests on a small number of treated patients.

evidence.snippet: Airway stenting was performed in 13 patients, all of which developed airway malacia.
evidence.explanation: Airway stenting is used for severe airway malacia in relapsing polychondritis.

evidence.snippet: Airway involvement in relapsing polychondritis (RP) can be debilitating and life threatening, often requiring interventional procedures.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the need for interventional airway procedures in severe, life-threatening airway disease.

treatments/5.description: For severe airway involvement refractory to medical therapy, interventional procedures (airway stenting, tracheostomy, non-invasive ventilation) provide structural support. Stenting is reserved as a last resort because it carries high rates of complications (granulation tissue, mucostasis) and is associated with worse survival; early biologic therapy is preferred to avoid it.

evidence.snippet: The pathogenesis of the disease is complex and still incompletely elucidated.
evidence.explanation: Authors explicitly note the pathogenesis is incompletely elucidated.

open_questions/0.rationale: HLA-DR4 association and a trigger-then-cryptic-antigen model are established, but the inciting triggers are only hypothesized (trauma, chemical, infection) and no quantitative gene-environment studies exist. The mechanism upstream of autoimmunity therefore remains the least-resolved step of the cascade.

evidence.snippet: proof of concept that RP is likely more than one disease
evidence.explanation: The VEXAS discovery is framed as proof that RP is more than one disease.

open_questions/1.rationale: The discovery that somatic UBA1 mutations account for ~8% of clinically diagnosed RP (the former "hematologic subgroup") demonstrates that the clinical label aggregates mechanistically distinct diseases with different demographics, prognosis, and treatment response. How to formally partition the entity is unresolved.

evidence.snippet: no randomised clinical trial has been conducted to date and treatment remains empirical
evidence.explanation: No randomized trials exist and treatment remains empirical.

evidence.snippet: there are no approved metrics to gauge the disease's severity
evidence.explanation: No approved severity metrics exist, a gap for both care and trials.

open_questions/2.rationale: Management is empirical with no approved therapies and no validated severity metrics; this limits both clinical care and trial design. Emerging diagnostic models and the upadacitinib randomized trial may begin to close this gap.

evidence.snippet: It may be asymptomatic in 19% of the patients which warrants the importance of screening.
evidence.explanation: Silent aortic involvement in ~19% motivates screening, but the optimal protocol is undefined.

open_questions/3.rationale: Aortic involvement is frequently asymptomatic but carries high mortality from dissection/rupture, so screening is clearly warranted; however, no evidence-based screening protocol (which imaging, how often, in whom) has been defined.

evidence.snippet: Recently, we identified mutations in genes encoding two different subunits of the renal alpha-intercalated cell's apical H(+)-ATPase that cause rdRTA.
evidence.explanation: The gene-disease assignment, naming the cell type and the membrane domain at which the pump acts.

evidence.snippet: Previous studies have suggested that mutations in ATP6V0A4 consistently result in a loss of function, impairing the hydrogen ion transport efficacy of V-ATPase and leading to distal renal tubular acidosis and sensorineural hearing loss.
evidence.explanation: States the loss-of-function direction that defines this disease. The same paper reports a contrary gain-of-function variant, which is recorded as a boundary in notes rather than as part of this entry.

steps/1.description: Biallelic loss of function in the a4 subunit of the V0 membrane domain of the vacuolar H+-ATPase. Like the B1 subunit, a4 has expression largely restricted to kidney and inner ear, which is why losing it produces a two-organ disease rather than the systemic failure a housekeeping pump subunit would cause.

steps/2.description: The pump cannot move protons across the apical membrane into the tubular lumen or, in the inner ear, into the endolymphatic compartment. This one failed transport step is the branch point of the entry: the renal and the auditory consequences both hang off it, and neither is downstream of the other. That architecture is what makes alkali therapy ineffective for the hearing loss.

evidence.snippet: LVAS is common in patients with dRTA and may influence the type and severity of hearing loss in these patients.
evidence.explanation: Records that a structural inner-ear abnormality accompanies the functional pump defect and may modify the auditory outcome, which is one reason the auditory arm is variable rather than obligate.

steps/3.description: Loss of the same proton pump in the inner ear, where it contributes to the acid-base composition of endolymph. In the mouse null the consequence is unambiguous, and it is the strongest mechanistic evidence available for this arm: the endocochlear potential is not merely reduced but absent. In humans the arm is variable, and when it manifests is the least settled question in this disease.

evidence.snippet: Primary distal renal acidosis (dRTA) is characterized by hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis due to failure in proton excretion, variably severe nephrocalcinosis and/or nephrolithiasis associated with hypercalciuria and hypocitraturia.
evidence.explanation: States the failure-of-proton-excretion to acidosis step and names the downstream renal consequences this node feeds.

steps/4.description: The kidney cannot excrete the daily acid load or regenerate the bicarbonate consumed in buffering it. The diagnostic signature is a urine that stays inappropriately alkaline while the blood is acidotic. No ontology descriptor is bound to this node - see notes.

evidence.snippet: Autosomal recessive distal renal tubular acidosis (rdRTA) is characterised by severe hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis in childhood, hypokalaemia, decreased urinary calcium solubility, and impaired bone physiology and growth.
evidence.explanation: Names the acidosis and the three downstream consequences this node points at, in one sentence.

steps/5.description: Sustained systemic acidosis, present from childhood and severe enough to be life-threatening untreated. Everything else in the renal arm of this disease is a consequence of it, which is why one treatment - alkali - addresses that whole arm and nothing else.

steps/6.description: Continued distal potassium secretion in the face of failed proton secretion, giving hypokalaemia that is occasionally severe enough to present as paralysis before the acidosis is recognised.

evidence.snippet: variably severe nephrocalcinosis and/or nephrolithiasis associated with hypercalciuria and hypocitraturia
evidence.explanation: Links the urinary chemistry directly to the calcification outcome this edge asserts.

steps/7.description: The stone-forming combination: more calcium in the urine and less of the citrate that keeps it soluble. Notably the mouse null for this gene is hypocitraturic without being hypercalciuric, so the two halves of this node are not obligately linked.

evidence.snippet: There was an increased prevalence of chronic kidney disease (CKD) Stage >=2 in children (35%) and adults (82%).
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the outcome this node produces, and the child-to-adult gradient is what makes it a progressive process rather than a fixed deficit. The cohort is dRTA of mixed genotype, not ATP6V0A4 specifically.

steps/8.description: Sustained medullary calcification and stone disease scar the interstitium, and renal function declines over time. This is the node the renal arm was missing - nephrocalcinosis is not an endpoint, it is the step by which a treatable electrolyte disorder becomes chronic kidney disease, and it is the reason the surveillance schedule exists.

steps/9.description: Bone as the acid buffer of last resort. Chronic mineral release impairs bone physiology in the growing skeleton and produces the growth failure that brings many of these children to attention in the first place.

evidence.snippet: severe hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis in childhood, hypokalaemia, decreased urinary calcium solubility, and impaired bone physiology and growth
evidence.explanation: Lists hypokalaemia among the characterising features of the disease.

steps/10.description: Low plasma potassium from continued distal potassium secretion, occasionally severe enough to present as hypokalaemic paralysis.

evidence.snippet: variably severe nephrocalcinosis and/or nephrolithiasis associated with hypercalciuria and hypocitraturia
evidence.explanation: Names nephrocalcinosis as a characterising feature and gives the urinary chemistry that produces it.

steps/11.description: Medullary calcium deposition, typically found on ultrasound at or near diagnosis, and the main long-term threat to renal function.

evidence.snippet: However, several patients with ATP6V0A4 mutations have developed hearing loss, usually in young adulthood.
evidence.explanation: The original characterisation of the auditory phenotype in this gene as late-onset.

evidence.snippet: Surprisingly, seven probands with ATP6V0A4 gene mutations developed severe early SNHL between the ages of 2 mo and 10 yr.
evidence.explanation: The observation that overturned the late-onset rule, and the reason the disease name says "with or without" rather than naming an onset.

evidence.snippet: There was one patient with hearing loss in patients with ATP6V0A4 mutations (n = 6).
evidence.explanation: A small contemporary audiological series in which the ATP6V0A4 auditory phenotype was the exception rather than the rule. It is the counterweight to the French series above, and the two together are why this phenotype is VARIABLE.

steps/12.description: The variable feature the disease name encodes. Originally described as preserved hearing or hearing loss beginning in young adulthood, then shown to begin as early as two months of age in some patients. Onset, not presence, is what distinguishes this from the ATP6V1B1 form.

evidence.snippet: Large vestibular aqueduct syndrome (LVAS) was detected in 6 (67%) of 9 patients whose radiological evaluation results were available.
evidence.explanation: Gives the imaging frequency in a dRTA cohort. The cohort is not restricted to ATP6V0A4 patients, so this is a dRTA-level rather than a gene-level frequency.

steps/13.description: A structural inner-ear abnormality found on imaging in a majority of imaged dRTA patients, and a candidate modifier of which patients become deaf and how severely.

evidence.snippet: Nephrolithiasis was more common with SLC4A1 mutations (42% versus 21%).
evidence.explanation: The 21% is the comparator group, which is where ATP6V0A4 patients sit. The figure is therefore for non-SLC4A1 dRTA rather than for this gene specifically.

evidence.snippet: Renal complications of hereditary dRTA include nephrocalcinosis, nephrolithiasis, medullary cysts, and impaired kidney function.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews names nephrolithiasis among the renal complications of hereditary dRTA.

steps/14.description: Discrete calculi alongside the diffuse medullary calcification. Reported in about a fifth of non-SLC4A1 dRTA patients, against roughly double that in the SLC4A1 form.

evidence.snippet: There was an increased prevalence of chronic kidney disease (CKD) Stage >=2 in children (35%) and adults (82%).
evidence.explanation: Gives the frequency in children and adults separately. The cohort is 340 dRTA patients of mixed genotype across 29 countries, so the figure is not ATP6V0A4-specific and the entry does not claim it is.

evidence.snippet: Renal complications of hereditary dRTA include nephrocalcinosis, nephrolithiasis, medullary cysts, and impaired kidney function.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews names impaired kidney function among the renal complications, independently of the cohort figure above.

steps/15.description: Declining glomerular filtration, present in about a third of children and the large majority of adults with dRTA. It is the outcome that makes the renal arm of this disease consequential beyond the electrolyte disturbance, and the reason surveillance is lifelong.

evidence.snippet: Additional manifestations include bone demineralization (rickets, osteomalacia), sensorineural hearing loss (in ATP6V0A4-, ATP6V1B1-, and FOXI1-related dRTA)
evidence.explanation: Names rickets and osteomalacia as manifestations, and in the same sentence names ATP6V0A4 among the genes whose dRTA carries sensorineural hearing loss.

steps/16.description: Demineralisation at the growth plate from chronic buffering of retained acid by bone. The adult counterpart is osteomalacia.

evidence.snippet: impaired bone physiology and growth
evidence.explanation: Names impaired growth among the characterising features of the disease.

evidence.snippet: There was an increase>0.5 units in z-scores for height and weight in 18% and 36% of the paediatric patients, respectively.
evidence.explanation: Reports growth z-scores improving on alkali therapy, which evidences growth impairment as a feature of the treated disease and shows it is partly reversible.

steps/17.description: Failure to thrive in childhood, frequently the presenting complaint, and partly reversible once the acidosis is corrected.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in the ATP6V1B1 and ATP6V0A4 genes, encoding subunits B1 and 4 of apical H(+) ATPase, cause recessive forms of distal renal tubular acidosis (dRTA).
evidence.explanation: States the gene-to-pump-to-disease link that this edge asserts.

edges/1.description: The subunit is a component of the pump that performs the secretion, so losing it removes the transport activity itself.

edges/2.description: Net acid excretion is the sum of the protons the distal nephron secretes, so removing the secretory step removes the excretion.

evidence.snippet: We show here that ATP6V0A4 is expressed within the human inner ear.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the gene is expressed at the site of the auditory phenotype, which is the evidence that the ear arm is a direct consequence of the pump defect rather than of the systemic acidosis.

edges/3.description: The same pump, expressed in the inner ear, contributes to the acid-base composition of endolymph. This edge is parallel to the renal one rather than downstream of it.

edges/4.description: Retained acid with preserved chloride handling gives an acidosis with a normal anion gap.

edges/5.description: Impaired distal proton secretion increases the electrochemical drive for potassium secretion in the same nephron segment.

edges/6.description: Acidosis mobilises bone buffer, raising the filtered calcium load, and increases proximal citrate reabsorption, lowering the urinary citrate that would otherwise hold that calcium in solution.

edges/7.description: Chronic buffering of retained acid at the expense of bone mineral.

edges/8.description: The wasting is the mechanism; the low plasma potassium is the measured phenotype.

edges/9.description: Calcium salts precipitate in the medullary interstitium once urinary solubility is exceeded.

edges/10.description: The same supersaturation forms discrete stones as well as diffuse medullary deposition.

edges/11.description: Calcification and stone disease damage the interstitium over years, which is how the renal arm reaches chronic kidney disease.

edges/12.description: Cumulative nephron loss presenting as reduced glomerular filtration rate.

edges/13.description: The systemic growth consequence of sustained acidosis and its skeletal buffering.

edges/14.description: Demineralisation at the growth plate, the radiographic form the bone lesion takes in the growing skeleton.

edges/15.description: Endolymphatic compartment enlargement accompanies the pump defect. The edge is drawn with unknown intermediates on purpose - the mouse shows enlarged endolymphatic compartments in a V-ATPase mutant, but nothing establishes the steps between failed proton secretion and the structural change, and in humans the association is with dRTA generally rather than with this gene.

evidence.snippet: They were severely hearing-impaired, as shown by elevated auditory brainstem response thresholds and absent endocochlear potential.
evidence.explanation: The mouse null gives the mechanistic readout human studies cannot - the endocochlear potential itself is abolished, which places the lesion at endolymph homeostasis rather than at a neural or conductive step.

edges/16.description: Failure of endolymph homeostasis in the cochlea, with loss of the endocochlear potential that drives hair cell transduction.

evidence.snippet: In 12 ATP6V0A4 kindreds, seven of 10 mutations were novel.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the private, family-specific character of the mutational spectrum in this gene.

genes/0.notes: The a4 accessory subunit of the V0 membrane domain of the apical H+-ATPase. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause this disease. The mutational spectrum is heterogeneous and largely private, with most reported variants novel to the family in which they were found.

evidence.snippet: The medical treatment is simple and involves an alkali load which allows curing the metabolic acidosis.
evidence.explanation: States the treatment and the consequence it corrects.

evidence.snippet: Long-term outcome is usually good unless the patient's compliance is low or alkalizing treatment is insufficient.
evidence.explanation: Makes adherence the determinant of outcome, which is the argument for the prolonged release formulation curated below.

treatments/0.description:
Bicarbonate and citrate salts given to replace the buffer the kidney cannot regenerate. Citrate preparations do double duty, since urinary citrate is itself the depleted inhibitor of calcium precipitation in this disease.
It treats the consequence and not the cause. The pump stays defective and the urine stays inappropriately alkaline. Critically, it does not act on the ear: the auditory arm is parallel to the acidosis rather than downstream of it, so correcting blood pH has no mechanistic reason to change hearing outcome.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Supplies the base the failed distal nephron cannot regenerate, correcting the systemic acidosis without addressing the transport defect that causes it.

evidence.snippet: Plasma bicarbonate and potassium levels were in the normal ranges at the different visits, respectively, in 69-86% and 83-93% of patients.
evidence.explanation: The efficacy result on the acid-base node this treatment targets, reported as the proportion of patients controlled rather than as a mean.

evidence.snippet: After 24 months of treatment with ADV7103, mean spine BMD z-score values significantly increased as compared with baseline (p=0.024).
evidence.explanation: Evidences the bone arm of the treatment effect. The study is an open-label extension with no control arm, so the comparison is within-patient over time rather than against an untreated group.

treatments/1.description:
A prolonged-release combination developed specifically for dRTA, addressing the thing that determines outcome in this disease - adherence to a frequently dosed, unpalatable alkali. Over 24 months it held plasma bicarbonate and potassium in range in most patients, and spine bone mineral density z-score rose.
Best read as a better treatment of the acidosis rather than a treatment of the disease. It acts on the same node the older alkali salts do; nothing in the reported outcomes bears on the auditory arm.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: The same target as conventional alkali, with a release profile intended to hold plasma bicarbonate in range between doses.

treatments/1/targets/1.description: Improvement in spine bone mineral density and in growth z-scores follows from sustained correction of the acidosis, so the bone effect is an indirect consequence of the acid-base effect rather than a separate action of the drug.

treatments/2.description:
Amplification, escalating to cochlear implantation as the hearing loss progresses. It is curated as a separate treatment from alkali because it addresses the other arm of the disease: the auditory branch is parallel to the acidosis, so correcting blood pH does nothing for it and the only available intervention is to compensate for the deficit.
This record is the reason the two-armed architecture is not merely a modelling preference. If the arms were in series, treating the acidosis early would be an ear treatment too, and it is not.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Compensates for the auditory deficit. It does not act on endolymph homeostasis or on the pump.

evidence.snippet: Agents/circumstances to avoid: Potassium-sparing diuretics should be used with caution or avoided.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews Management names the drug class to avoid in hereditary dRTA.

treatments/3.description: GeneReviews lists potassium-sparing diuretics among the agents to use with caution or avoid. This is counterintuitive, because the disease runs with hypokalaemia and a potassium-sparing agent looks corrective - but these drugs act on the same distal segment whose proton secretion is already failing, so the acidosis is worsened while the potassium is being chased.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: Avoidance is aimed at not compounding the primary transport lesion; nothing here corrects it.

evidence.snippet: We found statistically significant linkage with a locus on Chr 13 that accounts for about 20% of the hearing threshold variation in the backcross mice.
evidence.explanation: The mapped modifier effect. Graded INDIRECT because the mapping was done in Atp6v1b1 mice and this entry is about ATP6V0A4 - it establishes that genetic background modifies dRTA-associated hearing loss, not that it does so for this gene.

evidence.snippet: The abnormal inner ear phenotype of MRL- Atp6v1b1vtx/vtx mice was lost when the mutation was transferred onto the C57BL/6J (B6) background, indicating the influence of strain-specific genetic modifiers.
evidence.explanation: The strain-swap experiment, which is the cleaner demonstration - the same mutation produces deafness or not depending only on background. Same INDIRECT caveat as above.

open_questions/0.rationale:
This is the open question of the entry, and it is not a gap in whether the mechanism is real - the mouse null settles that with an abolished endocochlear potential. It is a gap in what modifies it. Four candidate explanations are on the table, and they are not equally evidenced.
Genetic background is the best evidenced of the four, and it is the one an ATP6V0A4-only reading of the literature misses. In Atp6v1b1 mice the auditory phenotype depends on strain: MRL mutants are profoundly deaf, the same mutation on a C57BL/6 background is not, and a backcross maps a Chr 13 locus accounting for about 20% of hearing-threshold variance. That is a demonstrated modifier effect on dRTA-related hearing loss, and it is the reason this discussion does not claim the variability is unexplained.
It is evidence about a different subunit, though, and the entry does not paper over that. No modifier mapping has been done for ATP6V0A4, in mice or in humans, so transferring the finding is an inference from one V-ATPase subunit to another - which is why the evidence item carries directness INDIRECT.
The other three remain candidates with no study discriminating between them: residual a4 function differing by allele, enlarged vestibular aqueduct acting as a structural modifier, and ascertainment, since a cohort recruited through nephrology will not audiometrically test everyone at the same age. The two human series cited on the hearing phenotype point in opposite directions - seven early-onset probands in one, one affected of six in another - without either being wrong.

open_questions/1.rationale: The mouse is a faithful model of the pump defect, the acidosis and the deafness, and it still develops nephrocalcinosis - but it gets there without the hypercalciuria that is standard in human patients. So the model cannot be used to test calcium-directed interventions or to reason about stone risk, even though it is the right model for the acid-base and auditory arms. The mismatch is recorded so the model's fidelity is not read as uniform across the three nodes it is linked to.

evidence.snippet: Most frequently, Rhnull phenotypes are caused by homozygosity of an autosomal suppressor gene unlinked to the RH locus (Rhnull regulator or Rhmod types).
evidence.explanation: Establishes the regulator type as the commoner route and that the responsible gene is unlinked to the RH locus, which is why Rh antigens can vanish while the RH genes are intact. It does not name the gene; the next item does.

evidence.snippet: In all patients, we identified alteration of Rh50--frameshift, nucleotide mutations, or failure of amplification--which correlated with Rhnull phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Names the lesion this node is named for. Rh50 is the RHAG gene product, and the alterations reported are the loss-of-function classes the node asserts.

evidence.snippet: Rhnull disease includes the amorph and regulator types that are thought to result from homozygous mutations at the RH30 and RH50 loci, respectively.
evidence.explanation: Assigns the two routes to their two loci in one sentence, which is the claim the split into two initiating nodes encodes.

steps/1.description: The commoner route. Biallelic loss-of-function variants in RHAG remove the glycoprotein required to assemble and traffic the Rh complex, so the Rh antigens disappear even though the RH genes themselves are intact and their transcripts are made. This is a failure of assembly, and it is the route the RHAG-knockdown experimental model reproduces.

evidence.snippet: The deficiency of Rh proteins on red blood cells (RBCs) from individuals of the Rh(null) amorph type are the result of homozygosity for a silent RHCE in cis with a deleted RHD.
evidence.explanation: States the haplotype architecture of the amorph type precisely, which is what distinguishes it from the regulator route.

evidence.snippet: Family study and Rh blood typings demonstrated clearly that the proposita was homozygous for a silent Rh gene complex (Rhnull of the amorph type) that she inherited from her parents who are first cousins.
evidence.explanation: Documents the amorph type arising from a homozygous silent Rh haplotype in a consanguineous family.

steps/2.description: The rarer route, and a different kind of failure. A silent RHCE inherited in cis with a deleted RHD means the Rh polypeptides are simply never produced. Nothing is mis-assembled because there is nothing to assemble. Reported families are consanguineous, as expected for a phenotype this rare.

evidence.snippet: The cultured red cells generated recapitulate the major alterations of native Rh(null) cells regarding antigen expression, membrane deformability, and gas transport function, providing the proof of principle for their use as model of Rh(null) syndrome and to investigate Rh complex biogenesis in human primary erythroid cells.
evidence.explanation: PARTIAL, and the gap is worth naming rather than glossing. The source reports loss of GAS transport function, while the annotation on this node is ammonium transmembrane transport. RhAG carries both, so the observation is consistent with the annotation without being a measurement of it. Graded accordingly rather than asserted at full strength.

evidence.snippet: The Rh antigen is a multi-subunit complex composed of Rh polypeptides and associated glycoproteins (Rh50, CD47, LW and glycophorin B); these interact in the red cell membrane and are lacking or severely reduced in Rhnull cells.
evidence.explanation: Enumerates the components of the complex and states that they are lost together, which is the claim this node makes.

evidence.snippet: we were able to reveal for the first time that RhAG extinction alone is sufficient to explain ICAM-4 and CD47 loss observed on native Rh(null) RBCs
evidence.explanation: Causal demonstration rather than inference: knocking down RhAG alone reproduces the loss of the associated surface proteins, establishing the dependency implied by the regulator-type genetics.

steps/3.description: The convergence point. The Rh complex is not a single antigen but a multi-subunit assembly of Rh polypeptides with RhAG, CD47, LW, and glycophorin B, and in this disease the whole assembly is missing or greatly reduced. That the associated proteins disappear together with the Rh polypeptides is what makes this a membrane structural defect rather than a serological curiosity, and it has been shown experimentally that removing RhAG alone is sufficient to drag the associated proteins off the surface with it.

evidence.snippet: Rh(null) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by an absence of Rh antigens and a varying degree of hemolytic anemia and spherostomatocytosis.
evidence.explanation: Links the absent antigens to the stomatocytic morphology and the haemolysis in one sentence, and records that severity varies.

evidence.snippet: Lentiviral modification combined with ex vivo erythroid differentiation was used to stably inhibit RhAG expression, a critical component of the Rh(rhesus) membrane complex defective in the Rh(null) syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Describes the engineered model in which the membrane consequences, including deformability, were reproduced from the molecular lesion alone.

steps/4.description: The red cell becomes a stomatocyte, with the characteristic slit-like central pallor, and loses the deformability it needs to squeeze repeatedly through capillaries and splenic sinusoids. This is the mechanical consequence of losing a complex that is tethered to the membrane skeleton, and it is reproducible in an engineered model as well as observable on a patient's blood film.

evidence.snippet: As a result, individuals with Rhnull suffer chronic haemolytic anaemia known as the Rh-deficiency syndrome.
evidence.explanation: States the consequence of the membrane defect and names the syndrome for it, which is exactly the transition this node carries.

steps/5.description: Shortened red cell survival, predominantly extravascular, with the spleen removing cells that can no longer deform enough to pass through it. This is the node at which the membrane defect becomes an anaemia.

evidence.snippet: As a result, individuals with Rhnull suffer chronic haemolytic anaemia known as the Rh-deficiency syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Names chronic haemolytic anaemia as the defining clinical consequence.

steps/6.description: Chronic haemolytic anaemia of variable severity, present from birth. Severity ranges widely between reported patients and is not predicted by the genetic type.

evidence.snippet: Rh(null) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by an absence of Rh antigens and a varying degree of hemolytic anemia and spherostomatocytosis.
evidence.explanation: Records the stomatocytic morphology alongside the haemolysis, in the authors' own compound term.

steps/7.description: Stomatocytes on the peripheral blood film, the morphological clue that points from an unexplained haemolytic anaemia toward a membrane disorder. Reported descriptions include spherostomatocytosis, reflecting a mixture of shapes rather than a single uniform morphology.

evidence.snippet: As a result, individuals with Rhnull suffer chronic haemolytic anaemia known as the Rh-deficiency syndrome.
evidence.explanation: PARTIAL: the cited sentence establishes chronic haemolysis, from which reticulocytosis follows as the standard compensatory response, but this source does not report reticulocyte counts in these patients directly.

steps/8.description: Raised reticulocyte count from compensatory erythropoiesis, the expected marrow response to shortened red cell survival.

evidence.snippet: Another example of rare red cells that failed to react with all anti-Rh and anti-LW antibodies was discovered in a Spanish woman suffering from a severe hemolytic anemia typical of the Rhnull syndrome.
evidence.explanation: PARTIAL: documents severe haemolytic anaemia in a patient with the disease, which is the process that produces jaundice, but does not report the sign itself. Curated at that strength rather than asserted.

steps/9.description: Jaundice from unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, a consequence of ongoing haem breakdown rather than of liver disease.

evidence.snippet: As a result, individuals with Rhnull suffer chronic haemolytic anaemia known as the Rh-deficiency syndrome.
evidence.explanation: PARTIAL: establishes the chronic extravascular haemolysis that produces splenomegaly, without this source documenting spleen size. Recorded at that strength deliberately.

steps/10.description: Enlargement of the spleen under the chronic workload of clearing abnormal red cells. Note that splenectomy is approached with caution in the wider membrane-transport disorder spectrum, so the finding does not straightforwardly imply the operation.

edges/1.description: Without RhAG the complex cannot be assembled or delivered to the membrane.

edges/2.description: No Rh polypeptides are produced, so no complex forms.

edges/3.description: Loss of the complex compromises the mechanical properties of the membrane.

edges/4.description: The morphological change is what is seen on the film. Recorded as its own edge because the shape abnormality and the loss of deformability are observed differently, one by microscopy and one by rheology, even though they are two faces of the same membrane defect.

edges/5.description: Rigid, abnormally shaped cells are removed from the circulation early.

edges/6.description: Destruction outpacing production produces the anaemia.

edges/7.description: Compensatory erythropoiesis raises the reticulocyte count.

edges/8.description: Reached through unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia from haem breakdown.

edges/9.description: The organ doing the clearing enlarges under chronic workload.

evidence.snippet: We report studies of two Japanese Rh(null) cases and describe three new missense mutations of RHAG, the locus that encodes Rh50 glycoprotein and modulates Rh antigen expression.
evidence.explanation: Identifies RHAG as the locus encoding the glycoprotein that modulates Rh antigen expression, and reports disease-causing missense variants in it.

genes/0.notes:
Encodes the Rh-associated glycoprotein, required for assembly and surface expression of the Rh complex. Biallelic loss of function causes the regulator type, the commoner form, in which Rh antigens are absent despite intact RH genes. Reported variants include missense changes in transmembrane segments and splice-site changes. Note the identifier: hgnc:10006, verified against the ontology. The source deep-research report gave HGNC:9881 for this gene, which does not resolve.
Distinguish carefully from RHAG gain-of-function variants, which cause autosomal dominant overhydrated hereditary stomatocytosis. Same gene, opposite direction of effect, different inheritance, different disease.

evidence.snippet: Family study and Rh blood typings demonstrated clearly that the proposita was homozygous for a silent Rh gene complex (Rhnull of the amorph type) that she inherited from her parents who are first cousins.
evidence.explanation: Documents the amorph type arising from a homozygous silent Rh haplotype in a consanguineous family, which is the route this record describes.

genes/1.notes: Encodes the RhD polypeptide. Silent RHD haplotypes, inherited together with silent RHCE, cause the rarer amorph type, in which the Rh polypeptides are not produced at all. Being RhD-negative in the ordinary blood-group sense is an entirely different matter and does not cause this disease.

evidence.snippet: The deficiency of Rh proteins on red blood cells (RBCs) from individuals of the Rh(null) amorph type are the result of homozygosity for a silent RHCE in cis with a deleted RHD.
evidence.explanation: States the genetic architecture of the amorph type precisely: a silent RHCE inherited in cis with a deleted RHD, which is why this record and the RHD record describe two halves of one haplotype rather than two independent causes.

genes/2.notes: Encodes the RhCcEe polypeptides. Silent RHCE alleles contribute to the amorph type alongside RHD, and a novel RHce variant has been reported as a cause of the syndrome.

treatments/0.description: The defining management problem, and it is logistical as much as medical. A person whose red cells express no Rh antigens will recognise essentially any ordinary donor unit as foreign, so compatible blood means Rh-null blood, which is among the rarest phenotypes recorded. Practical consequences follow: advance planning, rare-donor registry linkage, and where feasible autologous donation and storage during periods of stability, because a unit cannot be found at short notice.

evidence.snippet: As a result, individuals with Rhnull suffer chronic haemolytic anaemia known as the Rh-deficiency syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the chronic anaemia that transfusion supports.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Replaces destroyed red cells without altering the underlying membrane defect. Supportive rather than corrective, and constrained by compatibility.

evidence.snippet: Family study and Rh blood typings demonstrated clearly that the proposita was homozygous for a silent Rh gene complex (Rhnull of the amorph type) that she inherited from her parents who are first cousins.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates the family study establishing both the inheritance and the distribution of the phenotype within a pedigree.

treatments/1.description: Autosomal recessive recurrence risk, carrier testing within affected pedigrees, and something unusual to this disease: identification of relatives who may share the rare phenotype and could serve as compatible donors. The family study is simultaneously genetic counselling and transfusion planning.

open_questions/0.rationale: The clinical literature consistently describes a varying degree of haemolytic anaemia rather than a uniform severity, and the variation is not obviously explained by which genetic route produced the deficit: regulator and amorph types both abolish the complex and both give a range of outcomes. Candidate explanations include residual expression in the Rhmod phenotypes, differences in the rest of the membrane skeleton, splenic function, and unmeasured modifiers, but with a disease reported in single families the question has never been addressed systematically. It matters because prognosis at diagnosis currently rests on observation rather than on anything measurable.

evidence.snippet: Patient fibroblasts were indeed abnormally permissive for viral replication in vitro, associated with profound failure of type I IFN signaling and absence of STAT2 protein.
evidence.explanation: Directly demonstrates that STAT2 loss abolishes type I interferon signaling and produces a cell-intrinsic defect permitting viral replication.

evidence.snippet: Functional studies showed an impaired IFN-I-induced response and a defective IFNα expression at later stages of STAT2 pathway induction.
evidence.explanation: Confirms in an independent patient that complete STAT2 deficiency impairs the type I interferon-induced response.

steps/0.description: STAT2 is a required subunit of the heterotrimeric ISGF3 complex (STAT1-STAT2-IRF9) assembled downstream of the type I interferon receptor. Biallelic loss-of-function STAT2 variants abolish or cripple STAT2 protein expression and prevent ISGF3-dependent transcription, so type I interferon (IFN-alpha/beta) fails to induce its antiviral interferon-stimulated genes (e.g., MxA, ISG15, OAS1). Because type III interferon (IFN-lambda) signals through the same ISGF3 module, the mucosal IFN-lambda arm is likely impaired as well, whereas STAT1-dependent type II (IFN-gamma/GAF) signaling remains intact - distinguishing STAT2 deficiency from the broader STAT1 deficiency phenotype that also includes mycobacterial susceptibility.

evidence.snippet: the proband developed disseminated vaccine strain measles following routine immunization, whereas an infant brother died after a 2-d febrile illness from an unknown viral infection.
evidence.explanation: Illustrates the severe viral illness phenotype, including disseminated live vaccine-strain measles, that follows from failed cell-intrinsic antiviral immunity.

steps/1.description: Without an inducible type I interferon antiviral program, host cells cannot restrict viral replication. Clinically this manifests as severe viral illness and, characteristically, disseminated disease following live attenuated viral vaccines such as measles-mumps-rubella. The defect is cell-intrinsic and reproducible in patient fibroblasts, which fail to be protected by exogenous IFN-alpha (but remain responsive to IFN-gamma).

evidence.snippet: the proband developed disseminated vaccine strain measles following routine immunization, whereas an infant brother died after a 2-d febrile illness from an unknown viral infection.
evidence.explanation: Reports severe and fatal viral illness in STAT2-deficient siblings.

steps/2.description: Affected individuals are predisposed to severe, sometimes life-threatening, viral infections from infancy, which may be recurrent and require repeated hospitalization.

evidence.snippet: A picture is emerging of greater redundancy of human type I IFNs for protective immunity to viruses in natural conditions than was initially anticipated.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the type I IFN deficiency context (including STAT2) in which recurrent/severe viral infections arise, while noting variable penetrance.

steps/3.description: Recurrent viral infections occur as a consequence of the cell-intrinsic type I interferon signaling defect.

evidence.snippet: the proband developed disseminated vaccine strain measles following routine immunization, whereas an infant brother died after a 2-d febrile illness from an unknown viral infection.
evidence.explanation: Documents disseminated vaccine-strain measles after routine MMR immunization, the characteristic live-vaccine complication of STAT2 deficiency.

steps/4.description: A hallmark presentation is disseminated infection after live attenuated viral vaccination, classically vaccine-strain measles following measles-mumps-rubella immunization.

evidence.snippet: a novel case of complete deficiency of STAT2 in a 3-year-old child that presented with typical features of HLH after mumps, measles, and rubella vaccination at the age of 12 months.
evidence.explanation: Reports HLH (with subsequent MIS-C) in a child with complete STAT2 deficiency following MMR vaccination.

steps/5.description: A hyperinflammatory phenotype, including hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) and multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C), has been reported in complete STAT2 deficiency, implicating dysregulated interferon biology in hyperinflammation as well as antiviral defense.

edges/0.description: Failure of ISGF3-dependent interferon-stimulated gene induction leaves cells unable to establish a type I interferon antiviral state, permitting unchecked viral replication.

edges/1.description: Without ISGF3-driven interferon-stimulated gene induction, ordinary childhood viruses replicate unchecked, so infections that are self-limiting in an immunocompetent host become severe and sometimes life-threatening from infancy.

edges/2.description: Recurrence is a separate claim from severity and is curated separately: the defect is cell-intrinsic and permanent, so each new exposure meets the same absent antiviral response rather than an immunity built by the last one. The two phenotypes carry different HPO terms (HP:0031691 and HP:0004429) and different sources.

edges/3.description: The hallmark presentation, and the sharpest demonstration of the mechanism: an attenuated vaccine strain is attenuated only relative to a host that can mount a type I interferon response. Classically vaccine-strain measles after MMR.

edges/4.description: A hyperinflammatory arm reported in this disease, drawn from the viral replication node because uncontrolled viral antigen load is the usual trigger for HLH. The intermediates are not established in STAT2 deficiency specifically, and the reports are single cases.

evidence.snippet: Sequencing of genomic DNA and RNA revealed a homozygous mutation in intron 4 of STAT2 that prevented correct splicing in patient cells.
evidence.explanation: Identifies a homozygous splice-disrupting STAT2 mutation as the molecular cause in the founder kindred.

genes/0.notes: Biallelic loss-of-function STAT2 variants cause this autosomal recessive disease. Reported lesions include a homozygous intron 4 splice-disrupting mutation (Hambleton et al) and compound heterozygous c.C1528T (p.R510X, nonsense-mediated decay) plus c.G1576A splice variants (Moens et al kindred). STAT1-dependent type II interferon signaling is preserved.

treatments/0.description: Immunoglobulin replacement (including high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin during severe infectious episodes) has been used to provide passive immunity and anti-inflammatory effect in STAT2-deficient patients, particularly in childhood before the adaptive immune system has matured.

treatments/1.description: Because live attenuated viral vaccines (e.g., measles-mumps-rubella) can cause disseminated vaccine-strain infection in STAT2 deficiency, such vaccines should be avoided; this is a key agents/circumstances-to-avoid consideration once the diagnosis is known.

evidence.snippet: surviving STAT2-deficient individuals have remained generally healthy, with no obvious defects in their adaptive immunity or developmental abnormalities.
evidence.explanation: Documents the generally healthy interval course in surviving patients, the clinical basis for the type I IFN redundancy hypothesis.

evidence.snippet: A picture is emerging of greater redundancy of human type I IFNs for protective immunity to viruses in natural conditions than was initially anticipated.
evidence.explanation: Review across IFNAR1/2, STAT1, STAT2, and IRF9 deficiencies supports greater-than-anticipated redundancy of human type I IFNs for antiviral protection.

hypotheses/0.description: Although STAT2 is essential for type I interferon signaling in vitro, the clinical phenotype shows incomplete penetrance for severe viral infection and many common childhood viral illnesses run a mild course. This is interpreted as evidence that human type I interferons are more redundant for protective antiviral immunity under natural conditions than expected, with type I IFN-independent mechanisms of cell-intrinsic antiviral immunity compensating in most infections.

evidence.snippet: Here we report the identification of mutations in STX1B, encoding syntaxin-1B, that are associated with both febrile seizures and epilepsy.
evidence.explanation: Identifies STX1B/syntaxin-1B as the presynaptic-release-machinery gene whose variants cause the disorder.

evidence.snippet: Three additional nonsense or missense mutations and a de novo microdeletion encompassing STX1B were then identified in 449 familial or sporadic cases.
evidence.explanation: Defines the loss-of-function variant spectrum, including a whole-gene microdeletion.

steps/0.description: STX1B encodes syntaxin-1B, a plasma-membrane t-SNARE of the presynaptic release machinery. Truncating, in-frame indel, missense, and whole-gene-deletion variants reduce or impair syntaxin-1B function. Syntaxin-1B is chaperoned by Munc18-1 and partners with SNAP-25 and VAMP2 in the SNARE complex, so its deficiency degrades the fusion machinery.

evidence.snippet: Our results thus implicate STX1B and the presynaptic release machinery in fever-associated epilepsy syndromes.
evidence.explanation: Directly implicates syntaxin-1B and the presynaptic release (fusion) machinery in the disorder.

evidence.snippet: Neuronal SNAREs and their key regulators together drive synaptic vesicle exocytosis and synaptic transmission as a single integrated membrane fusion machine.
evidence.explanation: Establishes syntaxin-1B (a core SNARE) as part of the integrated fusion machine.

steps/1.description: Syntaxin-1B is one of the three core neuronal SNAREs whose calcium-triggered zippering fuses the synaptic vesicle with the presynaptic membrane. Impaired syntaxin-1B function degrades SNARE-complex assembly and disturbs neurotransmitter release, implicating the presynaptic release machinery in the disorder. This is the module's key conformance target — the fusion-machinery arm.

evidence.snippet: Video and local field potential analyses of zebrafish larvae with antisense knockdown of stx1b showed seizure-like behavior and epileptiform discharges that were highly sensitive to increased temperature.
evidence.explanation: A zebrafish model links stx1b loss to temperature-sensitive seizures, the mechanistic basis of the fever-associated phenotype.

steps/2.description: Impaired presynaptic release disturbs cortical excitatory/inhibitory balance, producing neuronal hyperexcitability with a characteristic temperature sensitivity: in a zebrafish stx1b-knockdown model, seizure-like behavior and epileptiform discharges are highly sensitive to increased temperature, mirroring the fever-triggered seizures in patients.

evidence.snippet: Here we report the identification of mutations in STX1B, encoding syntaxin-1B, that are associated with both febrile seizures and epilepsy.
evidence.explanation: Documents febrile seizures as a core phenotype of STX1B variants.

steps/3.description: Fever-associated (febrile) seizures, the hallmark early presentation, reflecting temperature-sensitive cortical hyperexcitability.

evidence.snippet: mutations in STX1B, encoding syntaxin-1B, that are associated with both febrile seizures and epilepsy.
evidence.explanation: Documents afebrile epilepsy in addition to febrile seizures.

steps/4.description: Epilepsy spanning generalized epilepsy with febrile seizures plus (GEFS+) and, in some individuals, a more severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy.

evidence.snippet: STX1BG226R, causing epileptic encephalopathies, strongly compromises the interaction with Munc18-1 and reduces expression of both proteins, the size of the readily releasable pool of vesicles, and Ca2+-triggered neurotransmitter release when expressed in STX1-null neurons.
evidence.explanation: Electrophysiology in STX1-null neurons shows an epilepsy-causing STX1B variant shrinking the readily releasable vesicle pool and reducing calcium-triggered release, which is the fusion defect this edge asserts.

evidence.snippet: leads to an unfolded protein unable to sustain neurotransmission
evidence.explanation: Shows the milder fever-associated indel variant acting through the same route - a syntaxin-1B protein that cannot support release.

edges/0.description: Syntaxin-1B is a core SNARE, so variants that unfold it, deplete it, or disturb its Munc18-1 interface degrade the fusion machinery itself.

evidence.snippet: Wild-type human syntaxin-1B but not a mutated protein rescued the effects of stx1b knockdown in zebrafish.
evidence.explanation: The rescue arm is what makes this a causal rather than correlative link: restoring functional syntaxin-1B abolishes the hyperexcitable phenotype, while the mutant protein does not.

edges/1.description: Degraded presynaptic release disturbs the excitatory/inhibitory balance of cortical circuits, and the resulting hyperexcitability is temperature sensitive.

evidence.snippet: epileptiform discharges that were highly sensitive to increased temperature
evidence.explanation: Establishes temperature as the trigger converting the hyperexcitable state into discharges, which is the fever dependence this edge asserts.

edges/2.description: Because the hyperexcitability is temperature dependent, a rise in body temperature is what tips the network into a seizure - the fever-associated presentation.

evidence.snippet: This work suggests a role for ultrarare STX1B variants in the pathogenesis of a broad range of both common and rare epilepsies.
evidence.explanation: A 23-family cohort establishes that STX1B variants cause epilepsy beyond the febrile presentation, supporting an afebrile epilepsy outcome of the same hyperexcitable state.

edges/3.description: The same hyperexcitability also produces afebrile, unprovoked seizures, so the disorder spans a spectrum from GEFS+ through generalized and focal epilepsies to developmental and epileptic encephalopathy.

evidence.snippet: Three additional nonsense or missense mutations and a de novo microdeletion encompassing STX1B were then identified in 449 familial or sporadic cases.
evidence.explanation: Defines the STX1B loss-of-function variant spectrum across a large cohort.

genes/0.notes: Variants include early-truncating, in-frame insertion/deletion, nonsense, and missense changes, as well as a de novo whole-gene microdeletion, consistent with a loss-of-function mechanism affecting syntaxin-1B.

evidence.snippet: The treatment outcome in this group was overall positive. More than 50% of patients were seizure-free without medication (17); the remainder were seizure-free with AED treatment (11).
evidence.explanation: In the GEFS+ phenotypic group, antiseizure medication achieved seizure freedom in every patient who needed it.

evidence.snippet: Seizures were pharmacoresistant in all patients except F18, undergoing on average 9 AED trials.
evidence.explanation: In the DEE phenotypic group the same class of medication fails, with an average of nine drug trials per patient.

evidence.snippet: We identified 49 individuals harboring heterozygous variants in STX1B (NM_052874.3). ... [In the developmental and epileptic encephalopathy subgroup:] Of note, F4 responded with a significant seizure reduction to the combined therapy of lamotrigine and valproic acid after several unsuccessful AED trials. After the administration of bromide, F14 showed a significant reduction in seizure frequency.
